# yyot v1 scope and release criteria ## State This is the revised v1 scope. The repository currently contains Git/Entire scaffolding only; no yyot application, deployed reviewer experience, or acceptance evidence exists yet. This document specifies required behavior, not implemented capabilities. Optimize for general browser-task capability and strong per-user security. Hermes Agent is the selected agent harness. Reuse its built-in messaging gateway and suitable tool integrations. TypeScript remains the user's preference for yyot-owned service and integration code where appropriate; run Hermes in its upstream runtime rather than reimplementing it in TypeScript. Hosting, browser/file capability, persistent storage, and per-user security integration still require validation. Slack is the v1 user interface, using Hermes' built-in Slack adapter. The user reported that Sahan approved Slack identity replacing the assignment's Google-only chatbot sign-in requirement. Reviewers use the deployed app in the demo Slack workspace through its invitation/entry link. Inference is owner-funded; reviewers need neither a checkout nor an OpenAI account. ## Architecture: shared team context and private personal execution One Slack app connects collaborative team conversations and isolated personal Hermes runtimes. The diagram describes logical responsibilities; the gateway and broker can be modules in the same trusted yyot service. Hosting and storage providers are not selected by this diagram. ```mermaid flowchart TD Slack["One yyot Slack app
Shared channels/threads and private DMs"] <--> Gateway["Trusted Slack gateway
Verify sender and conversation audience"] Gateway <-->|Shared conversation| Team["Team Hermes context
Partitioned by authorized channel/project audience"] Gateway <-->|Private DM routing| Broker["yyot authorization broker
Private dispatch and controlled publication"] Team -->|Request private work| Broker Broker -->|Owner-approved content and audience| Team Broker <-->|Sahan-authorized execution| Sahan["Sahan's isolated Hermes runtime
Private profile and durable data"] Broker <-->|Nishank-authorized execution| Nishank["Nishank's isolated Hermes runtime
Private profile and durable data"] ``` Collaborative team context is required in v1. Maintain two visibility domains: shared team context contains authorized channel/thread conversations, team decisions, shared goals/progress, and deliberately shared documents/results; personal context contains DMs, private memory, credentials, browser state, private files/artifacts, and private execution observations. Shared context must respect its actual workspace/channel/project audience; membership in a workspace does not reveal private-channel context. Collaborators can continue a shared discussion and plan without automatically sharing personal account access. The private boundary includes each user's full personal Hermes runtime and persistent personal data: DM transcripts/session databases, memory, learned skills derived from private work, private logs, credentials, browser state, working files, and private artifacts. Provision a separate runtime environment and private data volume per owner, backed by owner-scoped durable storage. The team conversation runtime gets only authorized shared context and has no direct access to personal homes, credentials, or browser sessions. Personal runtimes may read team context their owners are authorized to see. Never automatically copy personal transcripts, memory, screenshots, tool results, files, or learned skills into shared team memory. Private results use 1:1 Slack DMs until the owner approves the specific content and audience for sharing. Never expose platform/database/storage administrator credentials to model-generated code. Use one Slack bot with authenticated audience/sender routing, team Hermes context for designated shared channels/projects, and fresh personal profiles for private interactions. Keep the message sender, shared task/context audience, and private execution owner as separate application fields. A team request that needs personal accounts or files dispatches through an owner-authorized broker into that owner's private runtime. Another collaborator may contribute to the shared plan but cannot silently take over that execution, reuse its account authority, or approve on its owner's behalf. The team runtime receives safe status and owner-approved results rather than raw private observations. Keep bot credentials in the trusted receiving gateway rather than copying the bot token into personal runtimes. Admission must reject unprovisioned requesters instead of exposing a shared personal default. Hermes supports shared room/thread sessions and profile selection, but those settings do not implement per-request user authority or whole-runtime sandbox dispatch. Reuse the Slack adapter and routing primitives where they meet the boundary, and implement yyot-owned provisioning, private execution dispatch, access checks, and publication where necessary. Audit shared ingress logs, caches, queues, memory providers, and delivery-recovery stores: private personal payloads must not be retained in an unscoped shared store, while intentionally shared payloads retain their audience access controls. The trusted ingress necessarily handles messages in transit; Slack and configured model providers also process their respective message content. Pin and validate the Hermes version used. See [shared session settings](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/sessions/#shared-vs-isolated-group-sessions), [shared-bot profile routing](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/multi-profile-gateways/#routing-shared-bot-chats-to-profiles-profile_routes), [profile routing non-goals](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/developer-guide/multiplexing-gateway/#non-goals), and [whole-runtime Docker deployment](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/docker/). ### Context and storage ownership | Data | Owner or audience | Access rule | | --- | --- | --- | | Team conversations, decisions, task progress, and team memory | Authorized workspace/channel/project audience | Scope retrieval and persistence to that audience. A shared runtime must not mix conversations with different access boundaries. | | Personal DMs, memory, learned skills, execution observations, and logs | Individual user | Keep within the owner's personal runtime and durable private storage boundary; never load automatically into team context. | | Credentials, browser sessions, working files, and private artifacts | Individual user | Only the owner's authorized private execution may use them. Personal runtimes cannot access another owner's storage. | | Deliberately shared documents and approved result copies | Explicit destination audience | Share only the approved content. The source private file and account remain private; sharing a result grants no account authority. | | Routing, run, approval, and recovery records | Verified sender, execution owner, and conversation audience recorded separately | Trusted yyot code enforces these fields. Persist private payloads within their owner's boundary and shared payloads within their audience boundary. | Keep durable history, task recovery state, and retained artifacts independently of a running worker's scratch disk. A restart must restore the same owner/audience boundaries. The team runtime and each personal runtime receive only scoped storage access; platform administrator credentials remain in trusted infrastructure. The concrete storage provider and artifact layout remain open. ### Shared task to private work to shared result 1. **Collaborate in the team thread.** Sahan requests a report and Nishank adds requirements. Both contributions enter the authorized shared task context. 2. **Authorize the private part.** If the report needs Sahan's account or private files, the broker verifies his authorization for that work, requests it privately if needed, and binds the work to his runtime. It supplies only team context he is allowed to read. 3. **Execute under Sahan's authority.** His personal Hermes runtime performs the work. Nishank can contribute to the team plan, but cannot redirect, resume, or approve Sahan's private execution through a thread follow-up. A changed private operation requires authorization covering that change; consequential actions receive their own owner confirmation. 4. **Return private output to Sahan.** Results and raw observations remain in his private boundary. Deliver the private result or a protected artifact link through his DM; raw observations are not automatically sent to Slack. The team receives only status appropriate for its audience, without private account details. 5. **Publish the selected result.** Sahan approves the specific content and destination audience. The broker publishes that content and records it in the corresponding team context. Changed content or audience requires fresh approval; source files, credentials, and raw observations remain private. This flow lets a team coordinate work that each account owner authorizes and performs through their own agent. Delegating account authority to another collaborator remains outside v1. Hermes integration points, browser/file execution, secure handoff, deployment, and restart persistence still need implementation and validation. ## Now: required behavior 1. **Execute general tasks and collaborate.** Understand natural-language requests across unfamiliar websites using one general execution engine. Discover, download, inspect, transform, and upload files when the task requires them. In shared team conversations, collaborators can contribute to a common task and reuse authorized shared decisions/progress across turns and restarts. Site-specific product scripts do not constitute general-task support. 2. **Collect and reuse access securely.** Collect passwords, API keys, TOTP setup keys, card details when required, and browser login/OAuth access through secure input or handoff outside chat and model inputs. Persist encrypted credentials and browser-session state, reuse supported access across tasks and fresh browser runs, generate TOTP codes outside model inputs, and let the owner revoke access. Revocation stops affected active execution and invalidates saved access/session state. 3. **Enforce ownership outside the model.** Derive the message sender and audience from verified Slack identity and authorized conversation membership. Bind every private run, browser/session, credential lookup, file operation, private artifact, personal memory/learned skill, and private-history retrieval to its owner's isolated runtime/data boundary. Bind team history, memory, and shared artifacts to their authorized audience. Another participant's follow-up can contribute shared task context but conveys no authority over a collaborator's private execution or accounts. Keep model-generated code isolated from platform master keys and other users' resources. 4. **Work in the background and recover.** Acknowledge requests promptly, give brief useful progress, clarify only material details, and provide private human login/verification handoff when necessary. Persist the goal and progress across access expiration or failures. Resume after the owner supplies what is needed, without blindly repeating completed consequential actions. Support cancellation and bounded execution. 5. **Confirm and verify.** Obtain the owner's confirmation before a concrete consequential action such as a purchase, external message, publication, or deletion. Changed action details require fresh confirmation. Verify the actual website state or intended artifact before declaring completion. Keep private account observations and results private until their owner approves specific content and its audience for sharing. Persist approved shared results with that audience scope; an approval to share a result does not grant account or filesystem access. These controls are application and execution-environment responsibilities. Hermes chat-session separation, profiles, allowlists, prompt instructions, separate browser profiles, or encrypted secret storage alone do not prove isolation or prevent observation leakage. Validate ownership across Hermes memory, session recall, learned skills, file/browser tools, and any enabled background jobs. Disable features whose data or authority cannot be scoped safely to their owner. Document and test the actual boundaries. ## Four deliverables | Deliverable | Completion criteria | | --- | --- | | Runnable repository | Dependency locks, setup instructions, environment-variable examples containing no secrets, and relevant verification instructions are included and exercised. | | Deployed reviewer experience | The backend and execution environment remain available without the developer's laptop. Two reviewers can enter through the Slack workspace invitation/entry link and use the app independently without local setup or an OpenAI account. | | Approximately two-minute yyoreel demo | A real request, secure access collection or handoff, and verified completion are shown. Include reuse/recovery where practical. Inspect the exported recording for exposed secrets before sharing it. | | Access-management and known-limits note | Explain verified identity/isolation, secret and browser-session storage, TOTP, reuse, revocation, observation leakage limits, and unsupported cases. Distinguish implemented and tested behavior from planned behavior. | ## Release evidence 1. Complete real tasks on at least two different websites through the same general engine, without preselected site-specific product flows; verify destination state rather than relying on the agent's completion message. 2. Find the intended requester-owned sandbox file and complete a browser upload. Also complete download, inspection/transformation, and upload as one task; verify the uploaded file is the intended artifact. 3. Collect access and a TOTP setup key through secure input, then demonstrate credential/TOTP reuse with a fresh browser run. Test session reuse separately, and verify revocation prevents subsequent reuse. 4. Exercise expired access or a controlled failure, provide the required owner input, and resume the persisted task successfully without replaying a completed consequential action. 5. Demonstrate two users contributing to the same shared task and reusing authorized team context after restart. Run adversarial checks: forged owner/account references, cross-user private file/artifact requests, another participant's thread follow-up, private-history/memory/learned-skill retrieval, and copied approval/handoff controls must not obtain another user's authority or private data. Verify concurrent private executions remain independent, a collaborator cannot approve an owner's action, and changed action details cannot reuse an earlier approval. Inspect transcripts, logs, memory-provider writes, and delivery/cache records for audience-scoped persistence. Demonstrate an owner-approved result becoming available to the team while its source private file, credentials, and raw observations remain protected; a shared turn must not automatically consume private state. Done means the required behavior is implemented, the four deliverables exist, and this evidence passes with honestly recorded limits. A video, a happy-path upload, or a deployed chatbot alone is not completion. If a required capability remains unsupported, report that gap explicitly rather than marking v1 complete. ## Later Additional interfaces beyond Slack, delegated use of another person's accounts, advanced cross-team memory/grants, and the configurable coding-agent-style approval-policy UX are deferred until after v1. Basic shared team conversation/task memory and explicit sharing of selected results are in v1. Hermes' built-in channel adapters can be evaluated when additional interfaces are needed. Ordinary owner confirmations remain in v1. ## Next Prove the execution path before broader implementation: one Slack app using Hermes' adapter, two users contributing to shared team context, owner-authorized dispatch into a full isolated personal Hermes runtime/data volume, file upload, durable team context and private history/artifacts across runtime restart, private login handoff, and explicit publication of an approved result back to the team. Validate conversation visibility, execution ownership, and publication separately rather than assuming shared sessions, profiles, or a terminal backend provide the boundaries. Then build the required behavior and collect the release evidence. Obtain the user's review before external submission or contacting the founders; this scope update authorizes neither.

Another collaborator may contribute to the shared plan but cannot silently take over that execution, reuse its account authority, or approve on its owner's behalf. The team runtime receives safe status and owner-approved results rather than raw private observations. Keep bot credentials in the trusted receiving gateway rather than copying the bot token into personal runtimes. Admission must reject unprovisioned requesters instead of exposing a shared personal default. Hermes supports shared room/thread sessions and profile selection, but those settings do not implement per-request user authority or whole-runtime sandbox dispatch. Reuse the Slack adapter and routing primitives where they meet the boundary, and implement yyot-owned provisioning, private execution dispatch, access checks, and publication where necessary. Audit shared ingress logs, caches, queues, memory providers, and delivery-recovery stores: private personal payloads must not be retained in an unscoped shared store, while intentionally shared payloads retain their audience access controls. The trusted ingress necessarily handles messages in transit; Slack and configured model providers also process their respective message content. Pin and validate the Hermes version used. See [shared session settings](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/sessions/#shared-vs-isolated-group-sessions), [shared-bot profile routing](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/multi-profile-gateways/#routing-shared-bot-chats-to-profiles-profile_routes), [profile routing non-goals](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/developer-guide/multiplexing-gateway/#non-goals), and [whole-runtime Docker deployment](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/docker/). ### Context and storage ownership | Data | Owner or audience | Access rule | | --- | --- | --- | | Team conversations, decisions, task progress, and team memory | Authorized workspace/channel/project audience | Scope retrieval and persistence to that audience. A shared runtime must not mix conversations with different access boundaries. | | Personal DMs, memory, learned skills, execution observations, and logs | Individual user | Keep within the owner's personal runtime and durable private storage boundary; never load automatically into team context. | | Credentials, browser sessions, working files, and private artifacts | Individual user | Only the owner's authorized private execution may use them. Personal runtimes cannot access another owner's storage. | | Deliberately shared documents and approved result copies | Explicit destination audience | Share only the approved content. The source private file and account remain private; sharing a result grants no account authority. | | Routing, run, approval, and recovery records | Verified sender, execution owner, and conversation audience recorded separately | Trusted yyot code enforces these fields. Persist private payloads within their owner's boundary and shared payloads within their audience boundary. | Keep durable history, task recovery state, and retained artifacts independently of a running worker's scratch disk. A restart must restore the same owner/audience boundaries. The team runtime and each personal runtime receive only scoped storage access; platform administrator credentials remain in trusted infrastructure. The concrete storage provider and artifact layout remain open. ### Shared task to private work to shared result 1. **Collaborate in the team thread.** Sahan requests a report and Nishank adds requirements. Both contributions enter the authorized shared task context. 2. **Authorize the private part.** If the report needs Sahan's account or private files, the broker verifies his authorization for that work, requests it privately if needed, and binds the work to his runtime. It supplies only team context he is allowed to read. 3. **Execute under Sahan's authority.** His personal Hermes runtime performs the work. Nishank can contribute to the team plan, but cannot redirect, resume, or approve Sahan's private execution through a thread follow-up. A changed private operation requires authorization covering that change; consequential actions receive their own owner confirmation. 4. **Return private output to Sahan.** Results and raw observations remain in his private boundary. Deliver the private result or a protected artifact link through his DM; raw observations are not automatically sent to Slack. The team receives only status appropriate for its audience, without private account details. 5. **Publish the selected result.** Sahan approves the specific content and destination audience. The broker publishes that content and records it in the corresponding team context. Changed content or audience requires fresh approval; source files, credentials, and raw observations remain private. This flow lets a team coordinate work that each account owner authorizes and performs through their own agent. Delegating account authority to another collaborator remains outside v1. Hermes integration points, browser/file execution, secure handoff, deployment, and restart persistence still need implementation and validation. ## Now: required behavior 1. **Execute general tasks and collaborate.** Understand natural-language requests across unfamiliar websites using one general execution engine. Discover, download, inspect, transform, and upload files when the task requires them. In shared team conversations, collaborators can contribute to a common task and reuse authorized shared decisions/progress across turns and restarts. Site-specific product scripts do not constitute general-task support. 2. **Collect and reuse access securely.** Collect passwords, API keys, TOTP setup keys, card details when required, and browser login/OAuth access through secure input or handoff outside chat and model inputs. Persist encrypted credentials and browser-session state, reuse supported access across tasks and fresh browser runs, generate TOTP codes outside model inputs, and let the owner revoke access. Revocation stops affected active execution and invalidates saved access/session state. 3. **Enforce ownership outside the model.** Derive the message sender and audience from verified Slack identity and authorized conversation membership. Bind every private run, browser/session, credential lookup, file operation, private artifact, personal memory/learned skill, and private-history retrieval to its owner's isolated runtime/data boundary. Bind team history, memory, and shared artifacts to their authorized audience. Another participant's follow-up can contribute shared task context but conveys no authority over a collaborator's private execution or accounts. Keep model-generated code isolated from platform master keys and other users' resources. 4. **Work in the background and recover.** Acknowledge requests promptly, give brief useful progress, clarify only material details, and provide private human login/verification handoff when necessary. Persist the goal and progress across access expiration or failures. Resume after the owner supplies what is needed, without blindly repeating completed consequential actions. Support cancellation and bounded execution. 5. **Confirm and verify.** Obtain the owner's confirmation before a concrete consequential action such as a purchase, external message, publication, or deletion. Changed action details require fresh confirmation. Verify the actual website state or intended artifact before declaring completion. Keep private account observations and results private until their owner approves specific content and its audience for sharing. Persist approved shared results with that audience scope; an approval to share a result does not grant account or filesystem access. These controls are application and execution-environment responsibilities. Hermes chat-session separation, profiles, allowlists, prompt instructions, separate browser profiles, or encrypted secret storage alone do not prove isolation or prevent observation leakage. Validate ownership across Hermes memory, session recall, learned skills, file/browser tools, and any enabled background jobs. Disable features whose data or authority cannot be scoped safely to their owner. Document and test the actual boundaries. ## Four deliverables | Deliverable | Completion criteria | | --- | --- | | Runnable repository | Dependency locks, setup instructions, environment-variable examples containing no secrets, and relevant verification instructions are included and exercised. | | Deployed reviewer experience | The backend and execution environment remain available without the developer's laptop. Two reviewers can enter through the Slack workspace invitation/entry link and use the app independently without local setup or an OpenAI account. | | Approximately two-minute yyoreel demo | A real request, secure access collection or handoff, and verified completion are shown. Include reuse/recovery where practical. Inspect the exported recording for exposed secrets before sharing it. | | Access-management and known-limits note | Explain verified identity/isolation, secret and browser-session storage, TOTP, reuse, revocation, observation leakage limits, and unsupported cases. Distinguish implemented and tested behavior from planned behavior. | ## Release evidence 1. Complete real tasks on at least two different websites through the same general engine, without preselected site-specific product flows; verify destination state rather than relying on the agent's completion message. 2. Find the intended requester-owned sandbox file and complete a browser upload. Also complete download, inspection/transformation, and upload as one task; verify the uploaded file is the intended artifact. 3. Collect access and a TOTP setup key through secure input, then demonstrate credential/TOTP reuse with a fresh browser run. Test session reuse separately, and verify revocation prevents subsequent reuse. 4. Exercise expired access or a controlled failure, provide the required owner input, and resume the persisted task successfully without replaying a completed consequential action. 5. Demonstrate two users contributing to the same shared task and reusing authorized team context after restart. Run adversarial checks: forged owner/account references, cross-user private file/artifact requests, another participant's thread follow-up, private-history/memory/learned-skill retrieval, and copied approval/handoff controls must not obtain another user's authority or private data. Verify concurrent private executions remain independent, a collaborator cannot approve an owner's action, and changed action details cannot reuse an earlier approval. Inspect transcripts, logs, memory-provider writes, and delivery/cache records for audience-scoped persistence. Demonstrate an owner-approved result becoming available to the team while its source private file, credentials, and raw observations remain protected; a shared turn must not automatically consume private state. Done means the required behavior is implemented, the four deliverables exist, and this evidence passes with honestly recorded limits. A video, a happy-path upload, or a deployed chatbot alone is not completion. If a required capability remains unsupported, report that gap explicitly rather than marking v1 complete. ## Later Additional interfaces beyond Slack, delegated use of another person's accounts, advanced cross-team memory/grants, and the configurable coding-agent-style approval-policy UX are deferred until after v1. Basic shared team conversation/task memory and explicit sharing of selected results are in v1. Hermes' built-in channel adapters can be evaluated when additional interfaces are needed. Ordinary owner confirmations remain in v1. ## Next Prove the execution path before broader implementation: one Slack app using Hermes' adapter, two users contributing to shared team context, owner-authorized dispatch into a full isolated personal Hermes runtime/data volume, file upload, durable team context and private history/artifacts across runtime restart, private login handoff, and explicit publication of an approved result back to the team. Validate conversation visibility, execution ownership, and publication separately rather than assuming shared sessions, profiles, or a terminal backend provide the boundaries. Then build the required behavior and collect the release evidence. Obtain the user's review before external submission or contacting the founders; this scope update authorizes neither. "}}}

We can test whether its abilities generalize.

The current [v1 scope](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/V1_SCOPE.md:38) gives us useful acceptance checks, but two successful websites would only be an initial proof.

I’d adopt these five layers:

1. **Test representative task families.**  
   Cover finding/comparing information, filling forms, changing account state, downloading/transforming/uploading files, logging in, and recovering from interruptions. Start with roughly **20–30 tasks across several websites**, mixing short tasks with workflows requiring multiple abilities. That’s an initial sample, not a guarantee of coverage.

2. **Define success before running each task.**  
   For “download this CSV, remove duplicates, and upload it,” success means checking the resulting rows, uploaded contents, destination, and absence of duplicate uploads. The agent saying “done” is insufficient. Use independent checks of website state or artifacts; use human review with an explicit rubric for subjective results. This follows the functional evaluation approach used by [WebArena](https://www.cmu.edu/flame/research/2024/webarena.html).

3. **Test unfamiliar variations and repeat runs.**  
   Develop on some websites, reserve others for evaluation, and vary wording, data, layouts, and session state. Give yyot the goal without a scripted sequence of clicks. Repeat runs with fixed time/cost limits and record every attempt. Once we tune against a failed evaluation task, it becomes a regression test; we need fresh cases to keep measuring generalization.

4. **Deliberately exercise failure and recovery.**  
   Expire a login, interrupt an upload, restart immediately after submission, provide ambiguous instructions, and revoke access mid-task. Check whether yyot preserves progress, asks for the right help, and avoids repeating completed actions. Ownership, private-data isolation, and valid approvals are release requirements: a high task-success rate cannot compensate for breaking them.

5. **Record boundaries and keep updating them.**  
   For each capability, record success counts, conditions, human interventions, time/cost, failure reasons, and model/tool versions. Distinguish **verified under tested conditions, needs assistance, unreliable, unsupported, and untested**. A failure needs diagnosis: a missing tool, an agent mistake, and a website blocking access imply different limitations.

For example, the eventual report should say:

> “File uploads succeeded in X/Y runs on these sites. Ordinary file pickers worked; this custom uploader failed. Login handoff was needed in Z runs.”

That tells us much more than “yyot supports uploads.”

We should combine repeatable sandbox tests with real-site checks through the deployed Slack experience. Public benchmarks can supplement this, but our own tests must cover yyot’s complete workflow.

**Today, the verified state is scope only: yyot’s browser capabilities remain unverified until we collect execution evidence.**","phase":"final_answer"}]}]}

The assignment says the user supplies their **TOTP setup key once through secure input**, and the assistant generates codes whenever login requires them. It also requires keeping secrets out of chat and model inputs, and letting users remove stored access. :codex-file-citation{path="/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Downloads/Zonko Labs Engineering Assignment.pdf" purpose="source"}

**There are two different things here:**

| Thing | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Setup key** | A long-lived secret provided by the website when setting up authenticator-based 2FA, often inside a QR code. |
| **TOTP code** | A temporary numeric code, commonly six digits, calculated using that secret and the current time. |

TOTP stands for *Time-Based One-Time Password*. The calculation is essentially:

**Setup secret + current time → current login code**

The website knows the same secret, so it can calculate the expected code and check yours. The usual time interval is 30 seconds. [TOTP specification](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6238)

**For yyot, imagine this login flow:**

1. You connect a website account and provide its TOTP setup key through yyot’s secure form.
2. yyot stores that key securely for your account.
3. Later, yyot logs into the website and reaches “Enter your authenticator code.”
4. Its secure login tool calculates the current code and enters it automatically.

You therefore don’t have to open your phone and copy a code every time.

**“Agent” here means the overall software system.** A regular TOTP library performs the calculation. The LLM requests the login operation; the secure tool handles the secret and code without putting them into the model’s conversation.

A single temporary code cannot enable future code generation; yyot needs the **setup key** for that. SMS codes, email verification links, and push approvals are separate methods that the assignment explicitly allows to require your help.","phase":"final_answer"}]}]}

The current [v1 scope](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/V1_SCOPE.md:38) gives us useful acceptance checks, but two successful websites would only be an initial proof.

I’d adopt these five layers:

1. **Test representative task families.**  
   Cover finding/comparing information, filling forms, changing account state, downloading/transforming/uploading files, logging in, and recovering from interruptions. Start with roughly **20–30 tasks across several websites**, mixing short tasks with workflows requiring multiple abilities. That’s an initial sample, not a guarantee of coverage.

2. **Define success before running each task.**  
   For “download this CSV, remove duplicates, and upload it,” success means checking the resulting rows, uploaded contents, destination, and absence of duplicate uploads. The agent saying “done” is insufficient. Use independent checks of website state or artifacts; use human review with an explicit rubric for subjective results. This follows the functional evaluation approach used by [WebArena](https://www.cmu.edu/flame/research/2024/webarena.html).

3. **Test unfamiliar variations and repeat runs.**  
   Develop on some websites, reserve others for evaluation, and vary wording, data, layouts, and session state. Give yyot the goal without a scripted sequence of clicks. Repeat runs with fixed time/cost limits and record every attempt. Once we tune against a failed evaluation task, it becomes a regression test; we need fresh cases to keep measuring generalization.

4. **Deliberately exercise failure and recovery.**  
   Expire a login, interrupt an upload, restart immediately after submission, provide ambiguous instructions, and revoke access mid-task. Check whether yyot preserves progress, asks for the right help, and avoids repeating completed actions. Ownership, private-data isolation, and valid approvals are release requirements: a high task-success rate cannot compensate for breaking them.

| Layer | Shared or separate? |
|---|---|
| yyot Slack bot | **Shared:** everyone talks to the same bot |

| Personal Hermes runtime | **Separate per user:** Sahan’s instance and Nishank’s instance |
| Personal profile and data | **Separate:** chats, memory, credentials, browser sessions, files |

- Ask one question for material ambiguity.
- Let safety, accuracy, and explicit instructions override brevity.

L44: # Running Many Gateways at Once
L45: 
L46: Operate multiple cite19†profiles — each with its own bot tokens, sessions, and memory — as managed services on a single machine. This page covers the operational concerns: starting them all together, viewing logs across profiles, preventing the host from sleeping, and recovering from common launchd/systemd quirks.
L47: If you only run one Hermes agent, you don't need this page — see cite19†Profiles for the basics. And if your instances live on different machines that one desktop app should reach simultaneously, see cite22†Connecting Desktop to Many Hermes Instances .
L48: ## When to use thiscite33†​ L49: 
L50: You want this setup when you have two or more Hermes agents that should all be online at the same time. Common reasons:
L51: 
L52:   * A personal assistant on one Telegram bot and a coding agent on another
L53:   * One agent per family member or one per Slack workspace
L54:   * Sandbox + production instances of the same configuration
L55:   * A research agent + a writing agent + a cron-driven bot — each with isolated memory and skills
L56: Every profile already gets its own per-platform supervisor entry: a LaunchAgent (`ai.hermes.gateway-<name>.plist`), a systemd user service (`hermes-gateway-<name>.service`), a systemd system service when installed with `sudo hermes gateway install --system` (runs as the invoking user via `User=`), a Windows Scheduled Task, or an s6/Docker service — and the Desktop app spawns its own per-profile `hermes serve` backend. This guide adds the patterns for managing them collectively.
L57: ## Quick startcite34†​ L58: 
L59:     `
L60: 
L61:     # Create profiles (once)
L62: 
L63:     hermes profile create coder
L64: 
L65:     hermes profile create personal-bot
L66: 
L67:     hermes profile create research
L68: 
L69:     # Configure each
L70: 
L71:     coder setup
L72: 
L73:     personal-bot setup
L74: 
L75:     research setup
L76: 
L77:     # Install each gateway as a managed service
L78: 
L79:     coder gateway install
L80: 
L81:     personal-bot gateway install
L82: 
L83:     research gateway install
L84: 
L85:     # Start them all
L86: 
L87:     coder gateway start
L88:     personal-bot gateway start
L89: 
L90:     research gateway start
L91: 
L92:     `
L93: That's it — three independent agents, each on its own process, restarting automatically on crash and on user login.
L94: ## Alternative: one gateway for all profiles (multiplexing)cite35†​ L95: 
L96: The model above runs one process per profile. The alternative is a single multiplexing gateway: one gateway process — whichever profile launched it — becomes the sole inbound process and serves messages for every profile on the box.
L97: 
L98: The default profile's lifecycle verbs target that process. Named profiles can stop or restart just their own bots without stopping the host:
L99:   * `hermes -p <name> gateway run` while it is live attaches instead of starting a second process: it prints the host gateway's PID and served set and exits 0. If `<name>` is not served yet, it asks the host gateway to re-scan `profiles/` and attaches once the answer includes it; it refuses (non-zero) only when the host gateway cannot be made to serve it.
L100:   * `hermes gateway start --all` / `restart --all` mean the one host multiplexer. They never sweep every gateway process on the box; a profile that still runs its own gateway is reported, never killed, with the `hermes gateway migrate --multiplex` one-liner.
L101:   * `hermes gateway run --replace` takes over the process serving this profile, whichever profile launched it. When the host owner is another profile's standalone gateway (an unmigrated per-profile fleet) it never serves this profile, so `--replace` starts beside it exactly as a plain `run` does, instead of refusing and respawn-storming under the supervisor.
L102: An older Hermes wrote a systemd drop-in (`hermes-gateway.service.d/20-replace.conf`) that forced `--replace` onto the unit; `hermes update` / `hermes gateway restart` now remove that file. `hermes gateway run --force` starts a separate gateway without asking the host process at all (the escape hatch when it is wedged or answering wrongly).
L103:   * Under a service supervisor the attach exits 75, not 0 — systemd, s6 and launchd all restart a 75 after a short delay, so the unit keeps retrying and takes over by itself the moment the host process goes away.
L104:   * Two units started at once can both see no host process yet; the host lock decides which one runs, and the loser exits 75 and attaches on the retry. `--replace` does not skip that check (every generated unit carries it), only `--force` does.
L105: Multiplexing is on by default (`gateway.multiplex_profiles` defaults to `true`), with one safety rule: an unset flag is a request the default gateway settles at boot, never a verdict.
L106: Each start it runs the same preflight as cite36†`hermes gateway migrate --multiplex` and multiplexes only when the fold would have been safe — two or more profiles, no secondary still running its own gateway (live process or installed service, or under s6 a per-profile slot that is actually up), no duplicate bot credential, and no port-binding platform without a `/p/<profile>/` ingress.
L107: Unset means on: when nothing blocks, the gateway multiplexes and writes `gateway.multiplex_profiles: true` into the default profile's `config.yaml` (comments preserved) so the file says what the runtime does.
L108: Otherwise it comes up serving the default profile only and says so loudly on a host with other profiles: a boxed warning at gateway start naming the profiles that are not served, the blocker, and the fix; the same box in the `hermes update` summary and `hermes gateway status`; a banner in the dashboard (`/api/status` carries `multiplex_standalone_reason`). A single-profile install is not warned — there is nothing to serve. Nothing is written on a refusal.
L109: An explicit `true` bypasses migration preflight, except for a launching profile that opts out with `gateway.standalone: true`:
L110:   * `gateway.multiplex_profiles: true` (what the migration writes) multiplexes regardless of the preflight — you, or the migration, made the call.
L111:   * `gateway.multiplex_profiles` has one valid value right now: `true`, and it is written for you. An unset key resolves on and is made explicit in the default profile's `config.yaml`. `false` is retired: the gateway rewrites it to `true` in place and prints a one-time boxed notice at that start and in the next `hermes update` summary — never a silent flip.
L112: A per-profile gateway is `gateway.standalone: true` in that profile's own config (a temporary shim, not a supported topology) or `--force` for the boundary cases below.
L113:   * `GATEWAY_MULTIPLEX_PROFILES` in the process environment overrides the unset-key decision the same way an explicit `true` does.
L114:   * `gateway.standalone: true` in a named profile's own `config.yaml` (`profiles/<name>/config.yaml`) is a temporary compatibility shim (see cite37†below ): the host gateway does not serve that profile, and the profile runs its own gateway without `--force`. Its gateway serves only itself, even if `multiplex_profiles: true` is also set (see cite38†No new per-profile gateways ). Set on the default profile it is ignored with a warning — the default profile is the host gateway.
L115: There is no environment variable for this key.
L116: Other processes (`hermes -p <name> gateway start`, the dashboard, `hermes gateway migrate`) never guess how an unset flag was settled: they read the running default gateway's `served_profiles` record, and fall back to the explicit flag only when no gateway runs.
L117: ### When to prefer multiplexingcite39†​ L118: 
L119:   * A container/VPS deployment where N supervisor units, N ports, and N PID files are a burden.
L120:   * Many low-traffic profiles that don't each justify a full process.
L121:   * You want a single thing to start, monitor, and restart.
L122: One-process-per-profile is no longer a topology to choose implicitly: a named profile's `gateway install` / `gateway start` refuses without `--force` (see cite38†No new per-profile gateways ).
L123: A profile that still needs its own gateway while a multiplexing gap is open can set the temporary `gateway.standalone: true` in its own `config.yaml`; where a real boundary blocks the fold — a fleet split across UNIX users, or a `HERMES_HOME` outside `<default home>/profiles/` — every profile keeps `--force` as its path.
L124: ### Pinning the flagcite40†​ L125: 
L126: With the flag unset, the default gateway decides at each boot (above). To pin it, set it on the profile whose gateway runs as the host process (usually the default profile) and restart its gateway — `true` forces multiplexing even where the boot preflight would have held back (`false` is retired and ignored):
L127: 
L128:     `
L129: 
L130:     hermes config set gateway.multiplex_profiles true
L131: 
L132:     hermes gateway restart
L133: 
L134:     `
L135: Equivalently, in the default profile's `~/.hermes/config.yaml`:
L136: 
L137:     `
L138: 
L139:     gateway:
L140: 
L141:       multiplex_profiles: true
L142: 
L143:     `
L144: (The flag is also accepted as a top-level `multiplex_profiles: true` for convenience.) When multiplexing, the default gateway enumerates every profile, brings up each profile's enabled platforms under that profile's own credentials, and routes each inbound message to the profile it belongs to. Each turn resolves the routed profile's config, skills, memory, SOUL, and provider keys — credentials are never shared across profiles.
L145: The host automatically serves unparked secondary profiles. Use `gateway start` on a parked profile to bring it back online.
L146: ### Stopping one profile without stopping the hostcite41†​ L147: 
L148: For a named profile served by the host multiplexer:
L149: 
L150:     `
L151: 
L152:     hermes -p coder gateway stop     # park coder; other profiles keep running
L153: 
L154:     hermes -p coder gateway start    # unpark coder and serve it again
L155: 
L156:     hermes -p coder gateway restart  # reconnect coder with its current configuration
L157: 
L158:     `
L159: `stop` writes `gateway.parked` in the profile home before asking the host to stop that profile's adapters and exclude its cron jobs from subsequent ticks. The marker persists across host restarts. Its contents are ignored; an empty file is sufficient. Provisioning can pre-create `<profiles-root>/coder/gateway.parked` so an installed profile stays offline. Parking does not delete the profile, its sessions, or its scheduled jobs.
L160: `start` removes the marker, then asks a running host to serve the profile. Without a running host it removes the marker and follows the normal start path; start the host from the default profile if prompted. `restart` unserves and serves the profile without writing a parked marker, re-reading its config.
L161: On a parked profile with no live per-profile gateway, `restart` behaves as `start`: it removes the marker and hot-serves the profile (a gateway started with `--force` beside the marker keeps its own restart instead). These operations do not terminate work already dispatched by a cron tick.
L162: The host also rescans every 30 seconds: adding the marker by hand unserves the profile; removing it by hand makes it eligible again. If the control socket does not confirm the request, the CLI says so and the next rescan applies the marker state. Adapter teardown or connection can take additional time. `hermes -p coder gateway status` reports `parked (hermes -p coder gateway start)` while the marker exists.
L163: The launch profile cannot be unserved. The default profile's marker is ignored with a warning; its lifecycle verbs and the `--all` variants retain their whole-host behavior. A separately running `--force` gateway retains its own process lifecycle.
L164: The dashboard and Desktop Stop / Start buttons for a served profile do the same thing: Stop parks it (`/api/gateway/stop?profile=coder` spawns `hermes -p coder gateway stop`), Start unparks it while a host gateway is live, and `/api/status` lists `parked_profiles`. Start on a named profile that is not parked still answers `409` — it would need a gateway of its own.
L165: #### Parked vs `gateway.standalone: true`cite42†​ L166: 
L167: The two never apply to the same profile at the same time, and neither one implies the other:
L168: Profile  | Host serves it  | `-p X gateway stop`  | `-p X gateway start`
L169: --- | --- | --- | ---
L170: Served (default case)  | yes  | parks it (marker + `unserve-profile`)  | already served
L171: Parked (`gateway.parked` exists)  | no, until unparked  | already parked  | unparks (marker removed + `serve-profile`)
L172: Standalone (`gateway.standalone: true`)  | never  | stops its own gateway process; writes no marker  | starts its own gateway
L173: `gateway.standalone` wins: the host never writes `gateway.parked` for a standalone profile and never serves it, parked or not, so `stop` and `start` on that profile keep their per-process meaning. Parking is the multiplex-native way to take one profile offline — it is what closes the "per-profile stop/restart" gap the cite37†temporary shim was kept open for.
L174: ### No new per-profile gatewayscite38†​ L175: By default, one host gateway serves every profile, and a named profile does not get a gateway of its own. Without the opt-out below, `hermes -p coder gateway install` (or `start`, `run`, and the service step of `hermes -p coder setup`) refuses with exit 78 whether or not a host gateway is running right now:
L176: 
L177:     `
L178: 
L179:     ❌ Profile 'coder' does not get a gateway of its own.
L180: 
L181:       Exactly one gateway per host is the inbound process for every
L182:       profile. Starting a separate gateway for this profile would
L183: 
L184:       double-bind its platforms (two pollers on one bot token, port
L185: 
L186:       conflicts).
L187: 
L188:       Install or start the host gateway from the default profile; it serves this one too:
L189: 
L190:         hermes gateway install
L191: 
L192:       Or fold an existing per-profile fleet onto one host gateway:
L193: 
L194:         hermes gateway migrate --multiplex
L195: 
L196:       A separate per-profile gateway (for a fleet split across UNIX users or a
L197:       HERMES_HOME outside profiles/) needs --force:  hermes -p coder gateway install --force
L198: 
L199:       Temporary compatibility path while multiplexing gaps are closed: set
L200: 
L201:       gateway.standalone: true in profiles/coder/config.yaml,
L202: 
L203:       then wait for the host gateway to rescan (<=30s) or send its rescan-profiles control verb.
L204: 
L205:       (gateway.standalone is a temporary compatibility shim while multiplexing gaps are fixed;
L206:       it will be removed once they are — plan to fold this profile with `hermes gateway migrate --multiplex`.)
L207: 
L208:     `
L209: When the host gateway is already running and serves the profile, the first line reads `The host gateway already serves profile 'coder'.` with the owner's PID and served set, and the pointer is `hermes -p default gateway restart`. The dashboard's Start button for a named profile returns the same refusal.
L210: ### Temporary: `gateway.standalone: true`cite37†​ L211: 
L212: Temporary backwards compatibility, not a topology we keep
L213: Multiplex-only is the direction: one gateway per host serves every profile. The switch landed before every gap was closed — the WhatsApp bridge and relay on secondary profiles, and dashboard scoping are the open ones; per-profile stop/start/restart is closed by cite41†parking — and fleets that relied on per-profile gateways lost them overnight. `gateway.standalone: true` exists so those fleets keep working while those gaps are fixed.
L214: It will be removed once they are, with a release-notes notice ahead of time; every surface that prints it says so. Do not build new setups on it: if you are starting fresh, run the host multiplexer. If a gap blocks you today, set the key, and file or upvote the issue for the gap so we can remove the shim sooner.
L215: Set `gateway.standalone: true` in the profile's own `config.yaml`:
L216: 
L217:     `
L218: 
L219:     # profiles/coder/config.yaml
L220: 
L221:     gateway:
L222: 
L223:       standalone: true
L224: 
L225:     `
L226: The host gateway then does not serve the profile, and the boot log records `profile 'coder' is standalone (gateway.standalone: true); not served by this gateway`. `hermes -p coder gateway install|start|run` works without `--force`. If the running host still lists the profile in its served set, the command refuses until it rescans: wait for the next rescan (at most 30 seconds under normal operation), or send the `rescan-profiles` control verb to the host gateway. No host restart is required.
L227: Removing the key makes the profile eligible for the host again. While the profile's own gateway is live, the host skips adding it and logs that it must be stopped first. Stop that gateway; the host takes the profile on its next rescan.
L228: A standalone profile's adapters, cron, webhook ingress and Kanban notifications run only while its own gateway runs, not under the host multiplexer or `hermes serve`. Point webhook clients at the standalone gateway's own listener; the host's `/p/<profile>/` ingress no longer serves it.
L229: That listener resolves its port from the profile's own `.env` or `config.yaml`, so when both it and the host gateway enable the API server or webhook ingress, give the profile its own `API_SERVER_PORT` / `WEBHOOK_PORT`; two gateways left on the defaults both try to bind them. The cron destination picker still lists standalone profiles as `bot-chat:<name>` targets, but the host cannot deliver to those targets.
L230: `hermes -p coder gateway status` prints `standalone by config (gateway.standalone: true)` before the profile's own gateway state, and `hermes gateway status` (default) lists it as `standalone by config: coder` after the served set. `hermes gateway migrate --multiplex` leaves the profile alone and prints it as `Standalone by config (gateway.standalone: true), left alone`. The WhatsApp bridge and relay run in the profile's own gateway, as in any standalone gateway.
L231: `--force` is not the path for this shim; it remains the escape for the two boundary cases the refusal names (a fleet split across UNIX users, a `HERMES_HOME` outside `profiles/`): it installs a real per-profile service, and that service (its `ExecStart` carries no `--force`) keeps starting normally afterwards.
L232: ### What changes when multiplexing is oncite43†​ L233: 
L234: Multiplexing changes how a few things behave. None of these apply to a profile that opts out with `gateway.standalone: true` or runs a separate `--force` gateway on a blocked host.
L235: #### 1. Secondary profiles must not start their own gatewaycite44†​ L236: With a multiplexer running, a named profile's `gateway run` attaches to it; `gateway install` refuses to create another process (exit code 78). The CLI refuses before touching a service manager, preventing a permanently failed systemd unit or a launchd respawn loop. Use the per-profile `stop`, `start`, and `restart` commands above to manage a satellite inside the host. `hermes gateway stop` on the default profile still takes every served profile offline.
L237: The dashboard and Desktop app follow the CLI: for a served profile the "Stop" action parks it and "Start" unparks it (see above); "Start" on an unparked named profile answers `409` with the same explanation (rendered as an inline notice on the System page). "Restart" restarts the multiplexer (the process that actually serves the profile) instead of spawning a `-p coder gateway restart` that could only fail.
L238: Because that restart reconnects every bot on the device, both apps first ask "Restart the shared gateway? All bots on this device reconnect: default, coder, research" (the list is the running gateway's `served_profiles`) and report "Shared gateway restarted (3 bots)" when it completes. A standalone profile keeps the plain restart. `/api/status?profile=coder` carries the same list as `gateway_shared_with` (null for a standalone gateway).
L239: "Served" is read from the running gateway's own record (`served_profiles` in the default home's `gateway_state.json`), so it stays correct when the multiplexer was enabled only through `GATEWAY_MULTIPLEX_PROFILES` in the default profile's environment, or when profiles were added after the gateway started.
L240: The setup flows follow the same rule: `hermes -p coder setup gateway`, `hermes -p coder setup`, `hermes -p coder gateway setup` and `hermes -p coder import` configure the profile's bots but skip the "install the gateway background service" step for a served profile, printing "Profile 'coder' is already served by the default multiplexer" instead of registering a stray unit or plist that could only sit dead. Add the bot token and the running multiplexer picks it up.
L241: The multiplexer is the single inbound process; a second profile gateway would double-bind that profile's platforms. A profile that deliberately wants a separate process opts out with `gateway.standalone: true` (see cite38†No new per-profile gateways ); pass `--force` (accepted by `run`, `start`, `install` and `restart`) only where a boundary blocks the fold.
L242: The cross-profile lifecycle wrapper script earlier on this page is therefore not used in multiplex mode — manage the host or its named profiles directly.
L243: #### 2. HTTP-inbound platforms are reached via a `/p/<profile>/` URL prefixcite45†​ L244: 
L245: HTTP-inbound traffic for a secondary profile arrives on the default profile's one listener under a profile prefix, not a second port:
L246: 
L247:     `
L248: 
L249:     # default profile
L250: 
L251:     POST http://host:8644/webhooks/<route>
L252: 
L253:     # the "coder" profile, same listener
L254: 
L255:     POST http://host:8644/p/coder/webhooks/<route>
L256: 
L257:     `
L258: An unknown or unconfigured profile in the prefix returns `404`. The shared listener is the default profile's `api_server` port (or its `webhook` port when no API server is enabled); it serves three kinds of profile-prefixed paths:
L259:   * `api_server` and `webhook` are mirrored, never duplicated. `/p/coder/v1/...` and `/p/coder/webhooks/<route>` are answered by the default profile's own adapter under coder's scope. A secondary must therefore not enable `api_server` or `webhook` itself (the dashboard refuses with `409`; an `API_SERVER_KEY` or `WEBHOOK_ENABLED` in the secondary's `.env` wires the credential without starting a listener).
L260:   * Every other inbound-port platform runs in shared-listener mode. A secondary that configures Twilio SMS, LINE, Teams, BlueBubbles, Microsoft Graph, WhatsApp Cloud, WeCom callback or Feishu webhook mode gets its own adapter instance built without a port; the default listener forwards `/p/<profile>/<the adapter's usual path>` to it. See cite46†Inbound-port platforms under the multiplexer .
L261:   * WhatsApp (bridge) and Relay are shared ingress owned by the default profile. The multiplexer never starts them for a secondary: `WHATSAPP_ENABLED=true` in `profiles/work/.env` does nothing on its own. Enable and configure them on the default profile (their inbound is routed to profiles via `profile_routes`), or disable them in the secondary.
L262: The gateway logs one INFO line per skipped secondary platform, and if no profile runs it a WARNING says the platform is not being served; `hermes gateway status --profile work` shows `whatsapp: not served under multiplex (shared ingress owned by default)`. The one exception is a profile that opted out with `gateway.standalone: true` — it runs its own WhatsApp bridge and relay in its own gateway, as any standalone gateway does.
L263: Authentication follows the profile named in the URL. Unprefixed endpoints keep using the default listener's existing credentials.
L264:   * `/p/coder/...` API-server requests must use `API_SERVER_KEY` from `~/.hermes/profiles/coder/.env`; the default listener key is rejected. Under the multiplexer that key only authenticates the prefix — it does not turn on a second `api_server` listener in the secondary profile, so you do not need to pin `platforms.api_server.enabled: false` in the secondary's `config.yaml`.
L265:   * A webhook route that targets `coder` must declare `profile: coder` beside its existing route-specific `secret` in the default profile's `config.yaml`. That secret is then accepted only at `/p/coder/webhooks/<route>` and is rejected on every other profile prefix.
L266:   * Webhook routes without `profile` remain default-profile routes and are not reachable through a named profile prefix. Dynamic subscriptions bind the same way: `hermes webhook subscribe <name> --route-profile coder` writes `profile: coder` into the default gateway's `webhook_subscriptions.json` and prints the `/p/coder/webhooks/<name>` URL (`hermes webhook ls` shows the binding).
L267: Use `--route-profile`, not the global `-p coder`: `-p` would write the subscription into coder's own subscriptions file, which the default gateway's webhook adapter never reads.
L268:   * Delivery follows the same binding. A `profile: coder` route's reply (or `deliver_only` message) goes out through coder's adapter for the `deliver` platform, falls back to coder's home channel when `deliver_extra.chat_id` is unset, and a `github_comment` delivery runs `gh` with `GH_TOKEN` / `GITHUB_TOKEN` from `profiles/coder/.env`.
L269: If coder has no adapter for that platform the delivery fails (502) rather than posting as another profile's bot; a default route likewise never borrows a platform that is enabled only on a secondary profile.
L270:   * `/p/coder/api/platforms/<platform>/events` callbacks are verified and dispatched by coder's adapter; when coder has none the callback is a 503.
L271: Named API requests fail closed when the target profile has no `API_SERVER_KEY`. Security configuration errors remain fatal: for example, an `open` own-policy platform without `GATEWAY_ALLOW_ALL_USERS` or its platform-specific allow-all opt-in still aborts gateway startup rather than silently dropping the unsafe profile.
L272: #### Inbound-port platforms under the multiplexercite46†​ L273: A standalone `hermes -p coder gateway run` binds coder's Twilio, LINE, Teams, … webhook servers on their own ports. Under the multiplexer those adapters are still coder's — same credentials from `profiles/coder/.env`, same `config.yaml`, replies sent through coder's channel — but they bind no port. The default profile's shared listener forwards `/p/coder/<path>` to them, where `<path>` is exactly the path the adapter would serve standalone.
L274: The request is verified by coder's adapter with coder's secret (Twilio auth token, LINE channel secret, Teams app credentials, BlueBubbles password, …) and runs under coder's runtime scope; the default profile's own `/path` is untouched, and a profile that has no adapter for a path gets `404`, never another profile's bot.
L275: Platform  | Secondary profile's callback URL on the shared listener  | Verified with the named profile's
L276: --- | --- | ---
L277: Twilio SMS (`sms`)  | `https://<host>/p/<profile>/webhooks/twilio`  | `TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN` signature (`SMS_WEBHOOK_URL` must be this URL)
L278: LINE (`line`)  | `https://<host>/p/<profile>/line/webhook` (media: `/p/<profile>/line/media/...`)  | `LINE_CHANNEL_SECRET`
L279: Microsoft Teams (`teams`)  | `https://<host>/p/<profile>/api/messages`  | Bot Framework token for `TEAMS_CLIENT_ID`
L280: BlueBubbles (`bluebubbles`)  | `http://<host>/p/<profile>/bluebubbles-webhook` (registered with the server automatically)  | `BLUEBUBBLES_PASSWORD`
L281: Microsoft Graph (`msgraph_webhook`)  | `https://<host>/p/<profile>/msgraph/webhook`  | `extra.client_state`
L282: WhatsApp Cloud (`whatsapp_cloud`)  | `https://<host>/p/<profile>/whatsapp/webhook`  | `WHATSAPP_CLOUD_APP_SECRET` / verify token
L283: WeCom callback (`wecom_callback`)  | `https://<host>/p/<profile>/wecom/callback`  | the app's callback token / AES key

Message Type: FINAL_ANSWER
Task name: /root
Sender: /root/inspect_yyot
Payload:
Read all 22 turns in **“Enable Entire for yyot”**, thread `01a0f801-669b-7632-91cd-fec7b6e04b23`.

**The historical direction is one yyot product/bot with separate private agent runtimes per user, plus deliberately shared task context. “Same agent, different profile” is too weak if it means one unrestricted shared process.**

User decisions and evidence:

1. **General browser agent via Slack:** user defined yyot as a general AI agent capable of open-ended browser tasks, including finding/uploading sandbox files (`01a0f84d…`), then said “yeah now you got it” and requested a build plan (`01a0f84f…`).
2. **Collaboration without credential crossover:** user explicitly wanted shared channel task context, separate access, and no Sahan impersonating Nishank or using his credentials (`01a0f8d5…`).
3. **Owner approves sharing:** in that turn, the user selected **Nishank, as the account owner** to approve publication of private results. Coding-agent-style approval-policy UX was deferred in their explicit answer.
4. **Separate execution per user:** user paraphrased “meaning every user would get a separate container” (`01a0f90c…`); assistant confirmed one shared Slack app with each user's own Pi runtime/container, browser, files, and private history. That architecture was still proposed, not deployed.
5. **Multi-tenant concern clarified:** user asked whether Prateek joining would share the same underlying agent (`01a0f90d…`). Assistant distinguished shared code/model configuration from isolated live execution and owner-scoped resources. Invitations confer access to yyot, not to another user's account.

Historical changes/contradictions:

- This chat moved through Python Browser Use → TypeScript alternatives → Browser Use Pi. **It never selected Hermes.** Hermes appears only as the user's previous locally hosted setup.
- E2B and Cloudflare Containers were alternatives, with Browser Use Cloud considered separately for Chrome. **No hosting provider was proven or definitively locked.**
- An intermediate scope update moved shared task memory to later. That was an assistant action after an incoming cross-chat message whose body is absent from this read. **Current V1_SCOPE.md explicitly restores collaboration to v1**, so do not repeat that old deferral.
- “One collaborative agent” appeared in an assistant summary of product experience; subsequent per-user container discussion resolved the process/security boundary more concretely.
- The latest local scope strengthens the model to **full per-user Hermes runtime + private durable volume**, with separate team context/runtime and trusted dispatch. This is consistent with the original security intent and more precise than profile isolation alone.

Recommended wording for the direct question:

> **One yyot bot, but a separate private Hermes runtime for each user.** Everyone uses the same agent software; each user's personal memory, tools, browser, credentials, and files live in their own isolated environment. A separate team context lets them collaborate, and only owner-approved private results enter it. Profiles may help routing/configuration, but they are not the security boundary. This is the current design; it is not implemented yet.

L889: --- | --- | ---
L890: Telegram DM  | `agent:main:telegram:dm:<chat_id>`  | One session per DM chat
L891: Discord DM  | `agent:main:discord:dm:<chat_id>`  | One session per DM chat
L892: WhatsApp DM  | `agent:main:whatsapp:dm:<canonical_identifier>`  | One session per DM user (LID/phone aliases collapse to one identity when mapping exists)

L896: When Hermes cannot get a participant identifier for a shared chat, it falls back to one shared session for that room.
L897: ### Shared vs Isolated Group Sessionscite81†​ L898: 
L899: By default, Hermes uses `group_sessions_per_user: true` in `config.yaml`. That means:
L900: 
L901:   * Alice and Bob can both talk to Hermes in the same Discord channel without sharing transcript history
L902:   * one user's long tool-heavy task does not pollute another user's context window
L903:   * a running turn is keyed to the sender that started it, but `/stop` still reaches it — see below
L904: `/stop` means "stop what is running in this chat": it first tries the caller's own session key, then any live turn in this chat — other participants' runs in the caller's own thread included — authorization-gated, and never another room, workspace or profile. So an idle Alice's `/stop` can end a turn Bob (or a bot) started in the room she is in.
L905: A `/stop` sent from inside a thread is narrower: it reaches runs belonging to that thread and a room-wide run that carries no thread slot (the rolling-DM shape), but never another thread of the same channel and never a peer's per-sender top-level run.
L906: If you want one shared "room brain" instead, set:
L907: 
L908:     `
L909: 
L910:     group_sessions_per_user: false
L911: 
L912:     `
L913: 
L914: That reverts groups/channels to a single shared session per room, which preserves shared conversational context but also shares token costs, interrupt state, and context growth.
L915: ### Session continuitycite82†​ L916: Gateway conversations do not reset after inactivity or at a daily boundary. Use `/new` or `/reset` for an explicit new conversation; context compression remains automatic. Core ignores legacy `session_reset` settings, reset-policy overrides and reset-timer environment variables. If your config still sets `session_reset.mode` to `idle`, `daily` or `both`, gateway startup and `hermes doctor` warn about it.
L917: To keep time-based resets, install the catalog plugin that reads the same block unchanged: `hermes plugins install hermes-session-reset-policy`. Cached agents may be released to reclaim resources without replacing the durable conversation. Restart-recovery freshness limits automatic continuation, not the history loaded when you send a message.
L918: ### Session hygiene: why you should still run `/new`cite83†​ L919: 
L920: Because gateway conversations never expire on their own, it is easy to run one session for weeks. That works, but it quietly defeats the learning loop and inflates costs:
