L701: ### Repair Degraded Stored Promptscite70†​ L702: 
L703: Older builds affected by #122822 could let gateway hygiene or gateway `/compress` persist a detached maintenance agent's reduced-toolset system prompt over the live session. After the root fix in PR #122825 is installed, use `hermes sessions repair-prompts` to find rows that were already degraded.
L704: The scan is conservative: it only proposes a repair when the stored prompt is missing the `## Skill Safety` guidance and the persisted `tools[]` pin contains `skill_manage` (which always emits that guidance). Rows with no readable pin, or with a `memory`-only pin (which is also a legitimate `toolsets: [memory]` setup), are reported as unverifiable and are not changed by this scan; clear them explicitly by `SESSION_ID` if needed.
L705: A memory-only row also becomes repairable on its own: once the session is resumed, its `tools[]` pin re-pins the full tool surface, after which a scan sees `skill_manage` without the Skill Safety guidance and clears it.
L706: 
L707:     `
L708: 
L709:     # Report verified candidates and unverifiable rows; writes nothing
L710: 
L711:     hermes sessions repair-prompts
L712: 
L713:     # Clear verified degraded prompts after confirmation
L714: 
L715:     hermes sessions repair-prompts --apply
L716: 
L717:     # Machine-readable report
L718: 
L719:     hermes sessions repair-prompts --json
L720: 
L721:     # Non-interactive automation: apply and report the ids actually cleared
L722: 
L723:     hermes sessions repair-prompts --apply --json
L724:     # Explicit destructive override for one session (id or unique prefix).
L725: 
L726:     # This clears the stored prompt even when it is healthy.
L727: 
L728:     hermes sessions repair-prompts SESSION_ID --apply
L729: 
L730:     `
L731: Clearing the prompt intentionally stores NULL; the next turn rebuilds and persists healthy bytes, which causes one expected `Stored system prompt ... is null; rebuilding from scratch` warning for each repaired session. That warning is the consequence of this explicit repair, not evidence of a new corruption.
L732: 
L733: Run the repair only after the #122822 root fix is present; otherwise a later maintenance compaction can degrade the row again.
L734: A running gateway keeps each cached session's old prompt in memory, so restart the gateway after `--apply` (`hermes gateway restart`) for repaired rows to take effect.
L735: ### Repair State Crossed Between Profilescite71†​ L736: Every profile owns one `state.db`, and every gateway session key names the profile that owns the conversation (`agent:main:…` for the default profile, `agent:<name>:…` for a named one). Older releases could leave the two disagreeing — a named profile's rows written into the default store, a child session inheriting from another profile's row, a routing row copied into the wrong store, a Telegram topic or `/voice` setting saved without the bot's profile.
L737: Current versions put new state in the right place; `hermes sessions repair-profiles` settles what is already crossed.
L738: 
L739:     `
L740: 
L741:     # Report only — every store is scanned, nothing is written
L742: 
L743:     hermes sessions repair-profiles
L744: 
L745:     # Perform the repairs (stop the gateway first; a snapshot of every store is taken)
L746: 
L747:     hermes sessions repair-profiles --apply
L748: 
L749:     # Machine-readable report
L750: 
L751:     hermes sessions repair-profiles --json
L752: 
L753:     `
L754: What it finds and does:
L755: Finding  | Repair
L756: --- | ---
L757: `profile_name` disagrees with the row's own session key  | relabel from the key
L758: rows sitting in another profile's store  | move (with all messages) to the owning profile's store
L759: `parent_session_id` pointing at another profile's row  | sever the link; the row's own identity is kept
L760: routing rows outside the default store (under multiplexing)  | move to the default store; an existing row there wins
L761: routing rows / `sessions.json` entries for a profile that no longer exists  | delete
L762: Telegram topic bindings and voice-mode entries missing their bot's profile  | relabel from the sessions that hold the chat
L763: Two cases are reported but never repaired without being told what they are: rows keyed to a profile that does not exist (create the profile, or `hermes profile migrate-identity <old> <new>`), and `agent:main:…` rows inside a named profile's store.
L764: The latter are either the history of a gateway that used to run standalone for that profile (`--legacy-main rekey` gives them the profile's namespace) or default-profile chats that leaked in under a scoped write (`--legacy-main move` sends them to the default store) — the rows themselves cannot tell the two apart.
L765: `--apply` refuses while a gateway owns any of the stores (it holds the routing index in memory and would write it back), and is safe to re-run: a second run finds nothing.
L766: ### Convert the Store Between WAL and DELETE Journal Modecite72†​ L767: `database.journal_mode: delete` only applies to databases Hermes creates. An existing `state.db` that is already in WAL mode is never live-downgraded at open — other gateway, dashboard or cron processes may hold uncheckpointed WAL commits, and a downgrade underneath them destroys those commits — so Hermes keeps WAL and logs one `ERROR` per process telling you the configured `delete` did not apply. The self-service conversion is:
L768: 
L769:     `
L770:     # stop every process using the profile's store first (gateway, dashboard, CLIs, cron)
L771: 
L772:     hermes sessions set-journal-mode delete     # WAL -> rollback journal
L773: 
L774:     hermes sessions set-journal-mode wal        # back to WAL
L775: 
L776:     hermes sessions set-journal-mode delete --db ~/.hermes/kanban.db   # another Hermes store
L777: 
L778:     `
L779: The command refuses — naming each PID and command — while any process still holds the file or its `-wal`/`-shm` sidecars, switches the mode without waiting out openers (a holder that appears mid-way makes SQLite refuse instead of racing it), and verifies the file header reports the new mode. It reminds you to set `database.journal_mode` to the same value when the config disagrees, because the next open re-applies the configured mode.
L780: The holder scan is local (open-file tables on Linux/macOS, the Restart Manager on Windows), so it cannot see a process in another container or VM sharing the volume. If the scan itself fails the command refuses because it cannot prove the store is quiet; `--force` waives only that case after you have stopped every Hermes process yourself — a process the scan does find is always refused.
L781: Enabling WAL is also refused when the store sits on a cross-VM filesystem (virtiofs/9p), where WAL shared memory corrupts silently.
L782: ## Importing Sessions from Claude Code and Codex CLIcite73†​ L783: Started a conversation in another agent CLI? You can pull it into Hermes and continue it here. Hermes reads Claude Code's session logs (`~/.claude/projects/`, or `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/projects/` when Claude Code's config dir is relocated) and Codex CLI's rollouts (`~/.codex/sessions/`, or `$CODEX_HOME/sessions/`) — the foreign files are only read, never modified.
L784: 
L785:     `
L786: 
L787:     # Interactive picker across both tools, newest first
L788: 
L789:     hermes sessions import
L790:     # Limit to one tool, or point at a specific file
L791: 
L792:     hermes sessions import --from claude
L793: 
L794:     hermes sessions import --from codex ~/.codex/sessions/2026/08/15/rollout-....jsonl
L795: 
L796:     # Import-and-resume in one step
L797: 
L798:     hermes --resume @claude
L799: 
L800:     hermes --resume @codex
L801: 
L802:     `
L916: Gateway conversations do not reset after inactivity or at a daily boundary. Use `/new` or `/reset` for an explicit new conversation; context compression remains automatic. Core ignores legacy `session_reset` settings, reset-policy overrides and reset-timer environment variables. If your config still sets `session_reset.mode` to `idle`, `daily` or `both`, gateway startup and `hermes doctor` warn about it.
L917: To keep time-based resets, install the catalog plugin that reads the same block unchanged: `hermes plugins install hermes-session-reset-policy`. Cached agents may be released to reclaim resources without replacing the durable conversation. Restart-recovery freshness limits automatic continuation, not the history loaded when you send a message.
L918: ### Session hygiene: why you should still run `/new`cite83†​ L919: 
L920: Because gateway conversations never expire on their own, it is easy to run one session for weeks. That works, but it quietly defeats the learning loop and inflates costs:
L921:   * Memory only pays off at boundaries. `MEMORY.md` / `USER.md` are injected at session start, and `session_search` exists to recall what fell out of context. In a never-ending session everything is still in context, so the agent has no reason to consult memory — the "self-learning" machinery barely runs. Memory distillation (the save before reset) also only happens when a session actually ends.
L922:   * Cost grows with history. Compression keeps a long session functional, but every turn still carries a large (compacted) prefix. A fresh session with distilled memory is almost always cheaper than a month-old thread.
L923: Practical rule: end a session when you finish a task or topic. Run `/new` (optionally named, e.g. `/new payments-refactor`) at natural stopping points — daily or per-project both work. Before the reset, ask the agent to "remember anything worth keeping" if the work surfaced durable preferences or procedures; it saves memories and skills from the expiring session automatically, but an explicit nudge helps. Restarting the machine or the gateway is not a boundary — the same session resumes.
L924: See cite84†Memory for what gets carried across boundaries.
L925: ### Continuity After Crashes and Restartscite85†​ L926: 
L927: A gateway chat is designed to be one continuous session — compacted repeatedly as it grows — until you explicitly run `/new` (or `/reset`). This holds across gateway crashes, restarts, and updates:
L928:   * Session identity (routing key, chat, origin) is written atomically when the session row is created, on every creation path (`/new`, first message, `/branch` children). If that write ever fails, the very next turn's routing refresh repairs the row automatically.
L929:   * After a restart, the gateway re-resolves each chat to the session with the most recent actual activity — an older, stale row can never win over the conversation you were actually having.
L930:   * Recovery respects `/new` boundaries: if the most recent event for a chat is an intentional reset, recovery starts fresh rather than reaching behind the reset to resurrect an older session. Elapsed time alone never prevents recovery of a durable conversation.
L931: ## Storage Locationscite86†​ L932: What  | Path  | Description
L933: --- | --- | ---
L934: SQLite database  | `~/.hermes/state.db`  | All session metadata + messages with FTS5
L935: Gateway messages  | `~/.hermes/state.db`  | SQLite — canonical store for all session messages
L936: Gateway routing index  | `gateway_routing` table in `~/.hermes/state.db`  | Maps session keys to active session IDs (origin metadata, expiry flags)
L937: Legacy routing mirror  | `~/.hermes/sessions/sessions.json`  | Backward-compat mirror of the routing index, written when `gateway.write_sessions_json: true` (the default)
L938: The SQLite database uses WAL mode for concurrent readers and a single writer, which suits the gateway's multi-platform architecture well.
L939: 
L940: `sessions.json` is not the session list
L941: The gateway routing index lives in the `gateway_routing` table inside `state.db`; `~/.hermes/sessions/sessions.json` is a legacy mirror of it, kept for backward compatibility (disable with `gateway.write_sessions_json: false`). It maps messaging session keys (`agent:main:<platform>:...`) to active session IDs. It only ever contains gateway/messaging entries, so if you run a messaging platform you'll see only those (e.g. `agent:main:whatsapp:dm:...`).
L942: This is expected and does not mean your CLI sessions are missing. `hermes sessions list`, `/sessions`, and the dashboard all read `state.db`, which holds every session (CLI, TUI, and gateway). The `/save` snapshots under `~/.hermes/sessions/saved/*.json` are convenience exports, not the index.
L943: If CLI sessions genuinely don't appear in `hermes sessions list`, the cause is `state.db` not receiving them — run `hermes sessions repair` and watch for a `⚠ Session store unavailable` warning at CLI startup, which means SQLite persistence failed for that run.
L944: 
L945: Legacy JSONL transcripts
L985: ### Oversized-Transcript Guardscite90†​ L986: 
L987: Two limits stop a runaway transcript from being loaded into memory all at once (both default to `20000` active messages; `0` disables the guard):
L988: 
L989:     `
L990: 
L991:     sessions:
L992: 
L993:       max_resume_messages: 20000   # interactive resume (CLI / TUI / Desktop)
L994: 
L995:       max_export_messages: 20000   # one-shot in-memory export of a single session
L996: 
L997:     `
L998: 
L999: `max_resume_messages` bounds what the resume actually loads, not the whole history of the conversation:
L1001:   * Desktop's cold resume pages the transcript over REST and only holds the live tip segment in memory, so it is bounded by the tip alone. A long-lived chat that has been compacted many times (dozens of segments, tens of thousands of archived rows behind a small tip) is exactly what compression is meant to produce and opens normally; its footer message count reflects the stored lineage, not the live prompt.

L381: What is shared by design: the process, its PID/lock and `gateway_state.json` (default home), the one HTTP listener, and the `profile_routes` table (declared on the default profile).
L382: ### Which profiles are servedcite54†​ L383: `gateway.multiplex_profiles: true` serves the default profile plus every live named profile under `profiles/`, except the ones that opted out with `gateway.standalone: true` in their own `config.yaml` — a standalone profile runs its own gateway and is not enumerated by the host (see cite38†No new per-profile gateways ).
L384: (The former `gateway.multiplex_profile_allowlist` key is retired; a config migration removes it from `config.yaml`, and a profile you do not want served but that has not opted out is archived or deleted instead — `hermes profile delete <name>`, or move the directory out of `profiles/`.) Deleted profiles leave a tombstone and are never enumerated; a profile whose directory is gone is never recreated by a served turn, the cron ticker or log routing.
L385: The served set controls `/p/<profile>/` API and webhook prefixes, runtime status, profile-route eligibility, and which profiles the in-process cron scheduler ticks (the Desktop backend's ticker re-enumerates the same set on every cycle — a profile created or deleted while Desktop runs joins or leaves the ticked set without a restart — and stands down for any profile a running multiplexer or its own gateway already serves).
L386: A multiplexer started as `hermes -p <name> gateway run` always ticks its own profile's cron store as well.
L387: The served set is live. A profile created while the multiplexer is running (`hermes profile create`, the dashboard, Desktop or the TUI) is served at once: the creator pings the multiplexer over its control socket, and the multiplexer also rescans `profiles/` every 30 seconds as a safety net.
L388: The new profile's adapters are built the moment its `config.yaml`/`.env` carries a bot token (creators usually create first, then add the token), `served_profiles` in the default profile's `gateway_state.json` is updated, and `hermes -p <name> gateway status` reports it as served — no restart, and the other profiles' adapters and in-flight turns are untouched.
L389: Deleting a profile stops and unroutes its adapters the same way, and `hermes profile rename` unroutes the old name before the directory moves and hot-serves the new one (the old name is not resurrected by the adapters or the cron ticker that were still bound to it). The one-credential-one-poller rule still applies: a hot-added profile that reuses another profile's token is parked with a `duplicate_credential` error, never started as a second poller.
L390: ### Routing shared-bot chats to profiles (`profile_routes`)cite55†​ L391: Multiplexing selects a profile per credential (each profile's own bot token) or per URL prefix (`/p/<profile>/` for HTTP platforms). When several communities share one bot token — for example one Discord bot serving many guilds — you can additionally route specific users/guilds/channels/threads to different profiles with `gateway.profile_routes`:
L392: 
L393:     `
L394: 
L395:     gateway:
L396: 
L397:       multiplex_profiles: true
L398: 
L399:       profile_routes:
L400: 
L401:         # An entire Discord server → one profile
L402:         - name: acme-server
L403: 
L404:           platform: discord
L405: 
L406:           guild_id: "1234567890"
L407: 
L408:           profile: acme
L409: 
L410:         # One channel in that server → a different profile
L411: 
L412:         - name: acme-support
L413: 
L414:           platform: discord
L415: 
L416:           guild_id: "1234567890"
L417: 
L418:           chat_id: "9876543210"
L419: 
L420:           profile: acme-support
L421: 
L422:         # A Telegram group (no guild concept — chat_id only)
L423: 
L424:         - name: tg-group
L425: 
L426:           platform: telegram
L427:           chat_id: "-1001234567890"
L428: 
L429:           profile: tg-profile
L430: 
L431:         # A WhatsApp DM — write the phone number; JID and LID forms also match
L432: 
L433:         - name: owner-whatsapp
L434: 
L435:           platform: whatsapp
L436: 
L437:           chat_id: "15551234567"
L438: 
L439:           profile: owner
L440: 
L441:         # One Teams user across DMs, groups, and channels (exact sender id)
L442: 
L443:         - name: teams-owner
L444: 
L445:           platform: teams
L446: 
L447:           user_id: "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000"
L448:           profile: owner
L449: 
L450:     `
L451: Routes are matched by additive specificity: `user_id` = 16, `thread_id` = 8, `chat_id` = 4, and `guild_id` = 2. Thus `user_id + chat_id` (20) outranks `user_id` alone (16), which outranks every location-only route (at most 14). All declared fields must hold (AND), equal scores keep declaration order, and a route keyed on a channel also matches threads/forum posts whose parent is that channel. Messages that match no route stay on the default/active profile.
L452: The routed profile gets the full per-profile isolation described above (config, skills, memory, credentials, session namespace). Routing works on every platform adapter, not just Discord.
L453: `user_id` is the sender of the inbound message, compared for exact equality. It is only as trustworthy as the adapter that reports it, so treat it as an authorization input only on platforms whose ingress authenticates the sender.
L454: Sender ids are also namespaced per tenant on some platforms — a Slack user id is workspace-local — so on a gateway serving more than one workspace or server, pair `user_id` with the `guild_id` of that scope (Discord guild, Slack workspace, Matrix server) rather than relying on the id alone.
L455: Omitting `user_id` keeps the route unconstrained by sender for backward compatibility. Setting it to `null`, an empty string, or whitespace invalidates that route instead of broadening it to every sender on the platform.
L456: Sender routing selects a profile; it is not deny-by-default authorization. A sender that matches no route falls through to the default/active profile, exactly like an unrouted channel. To give one person a privileged profile and everyone else a restricted one, declare the privileged sender route first, add a platform-wide catch-all route to the restricted profile after it, and keep the platform's own ingress allowlist in place.
L474: On WhatsApp and WhatsApp Cloud, a `chat_id` route matches across user-identity forms: a bare phone number (`15551234567`), a JID (`15551234567@s.whatsapp.net`), and a LID (`…@lid`) all refer to the same person once the bridge has paired them (the same canonicalization session keys and adapter allowlists already use). You can put the phone number in `profile_routes` and inbound DMs still match whether WhatsApp delivers a JID or a LID.
L476: `profile_routes` requires `gateway.multiplex_profiles: true`; with multiplexing off the routes are ignored. If an explicit route matches but its target profile is not installed (or was deleted), the gateway rejects that ingress and logs the route and target. It does not run the default profile. Traffic that matches no route keeps the historical default-profile behavior.

L44: # Profiles: Running Multiple Agents
L45: 
L46: Run multiple independent Hermes agents on the same machine — each with its own config, API keys, memory, sessions, skills, and gateway state.
L47: ## What are profiles?cite33†​ L48: A profile is a separate Hermes home directory. Each profile gets its own directory containing its own `config.yaml`, `.env`, `SOUL.md`, memories, sessions, skills, cron jobs, and state database. Hermes recognises a directory under `~/.hermes/profiles/` as a profile only when it carries one of those identity files (`config.yaml`, `.env`, `SOUL.md`, `profile.yaml`, `auth.json`, `state.db`); a bare directory left behind by logging or cron is ignored by `profile list`, gateways and `-p`.
L49: Profiles let you run separate agents for different purposes — a coding assistant, a personal bot, a research agent — without mixing up Hermes state.
L50: Give every agent its own profile
L51: 
L52: Never point two agent processes at the same profile (the same Hermes home). Both write memory automatically, and each loads the other's writes into its system prompt at session start — so two writers on one home compound each other's state until it stops being anything you configured. Profiles exist exactly to prevent this; agents that need shared memory should use an cite34†external memory provider instead.
L53: When you create a profile, it automatically becomes its own command. Create a profile called `coder` and you immediately have `coder chat`, `coder setup`, `coder gateway start`, etc.
L54: ### Profiles, agents, and botscite35†​ L55: 
L56: These terms describe different parts of Hermes:
L57: 
L58:   * Profile is the persistent home for an assistant's configuration and data. It keeps the same state across conversations and restarts.
L59: 
L60:   * Agent is the running Hermes assistant that uses that configuration and state. "Hermes Agent" also names the product.
L61:   * Bot Mode bot is a profile presented as a named entry in the desktop's cite8†Bot Mode roster, with an avatar and a persistent Bot Chat. The same profile remains accessible from the CLI. Every Bot is a profile, but not every profile is a Bot: a profile becomes a Bot when Bot Mode stores its roster presentation (title, avatar, section, hidden state) in the profile's metadata and pins its canonical Bot Chat.
L62: A profile you only ever drive from the CLI, Docker, or a gateway and never add to the roster stays a plain profile.
L63:   * Messaging bot is an account on a platform such as Telegram, Discord, or Slack, connected to Hermes through the gateway. Its cite36†bot token identifies that platform account.
L64: 
L65:   * Subagent is a child assistant spawned by cite37†`delegate_task` for a task, with a fresh conversation. A separate conversation is different from a separate profile.
L66: ## Quick startcite38†​ L67: 
L68:     `
L69: 
L70:     hermes profile create coder       # creates profile + "coder" command alias
L71: 
L72:     coder setup                       # configure API keys and model
L73: 
L74:     coder chat                        # start chatting
L75: 
L76:     `
L77: 
L78: That's it. `coder` is now its own Hermes profile with its own config, memory, and state.
L79: 
L80: ## Creating a profilecite39†​ L81: 
L82: tip
L83: 
L84: Quickest setup: run `hermes setup --portal` inside the new profile to wire up models + tools at once. See cite40†Nous Portal .
L85: ### Blank profilecite41†​ L86: 
L87:     `
L88: 
L89:     hermes profile create mybot
L90: 
L91:     `
L92: 
L93: Creates a fresh profile with bundled skills seeded. Run `mybot setup` to configure API keys, model, and gateway tokens.
L94: If you plan to use this profile as a kanban worker (or want the kanban orchestrator to route work to it), pass `--description "<role>"` at create time so the orchestrator knows what it's good at:
L95: 
L96:     `
L97: 
L98:     hermes profile create researcher --description "Reads source code and external docs, writes findings."
L99: 
L100:     `
L101: 
L102: You can also set or auto-generate the description later with `hermes profile describe` — see the cite42†Kanban guide for the full routing model.
L103: ### Clone config only (`--clone`)cite43†​ L104: 
L105:     `
L106: 
L107:     hermes profile create work --clone
L108: 
L109:     `
L110: Copies your current profile's `config.yaml`, `.env`, `SOUL.md`, skills, and the curated memory files `memories/MEMORY.md` and `memories/USER.md` into the new profile — memory is treated as part of the agent's identity, like `SOUL.md`. If `config.yaml` selects an external memory provider (`memory.provider`), that provider's own config travels too — its `<provider>/` directory or `<provider>.json` under the profile home, e.g.
L111: `hindsight/config.json` — so the clone's memory is available instead of silently off; a cloned `local_embedded` hindsight config still shares the source's embedded daemon and bank until you give the clone its own hindsight `profile`/`bank_id` (cite44†#81815†github.com ).
L112: Installed plugins travel too: `plugins/` (catalog, Git and hand-installed plugins, plus their install records) is copied, so a memory provider installed from the plugin catalog keeps working in the clone at the same revision and keeps its catalog install record. Plugin Python dependencies live in the shared environment and are not reinstalled. Sessions, `state.db`, cron jobs and everything else start empty.
L113: For a blank memory as well, create the profile without `--clone` or delete the two files afterwards; the agent never falls back to another profile's memory when they are absent. Edit `~/.hermes/profiles/work/.env` for different API keys, or `~/.hermes/profiles/work/SOUL.md` for a different personality.
L114: #### Keep a clone's imported agent setups synced (`--sync-imports`)cite45†​ L115: If the source profile has run cite46†`hermes import-agent` , its `import-sync.json` records which external Claude Code / Codex trees it imported. `--clone` leaves that manifest behind, so the clone gets a one-off copy of those skills and memories and stops there. Add `--sync-imports` to carry the manifest over:
L116: 
L117:     `
L118: 
L119:     hermes profile create work --clone --sync-imports
L120: 
L121:     hermes -p work import-agent --sync        # pulls changes from the same ~/.claude / ~/.codex
L122: 
L123:     `
L124: This is explicit, opt-in and one-directional, and it links the clone to the external agent trees only — never to the source profile. Both profiles stay independent islands: editing the source's `config.yaml`, `SOUL.md` or skills afterwards never reaches the clone. `--clone-all` copies the manifest as part of the full copy.
L125: ### Clone everything (`--clone-all`)cite47†​ L126: 
L127:     `
L128: 
L129:     hermes profile create backup --clone-all
L130: 
L131:     `
L132: Copies everything — config, API keys, personality, all memories, skills, plugins. A complete working snapshot. Per-profile history is excluded (session history, `state.db`, `backups/`, `state-snapshots/`, `checkpoints/`) — these belong to the source profile and can reach tens of GB. When cloning from the default profile, the local-model runtime trees (`models/`, `runtimes/`, `node/` — downloaded weights and managed binaries, re-fetched on demand) are skipped too, as `hermes backup` already does.
L133: Cron jobs are not cloned either: they are scheduled work bound to the source profile and its delivery channel, and a clone that inherited them would run every job twice (two gateways, same job ids). The new profile starts with an empty `cron/`. For a full backup including history and cron jobs, use `hermes profile export` or `hermes backup` instead.
L134: OAuth logins are shared, not copied
L135: Anthropic (Claude Pro/Max), OpenAI Codex, and xAI OAuth logins use single-use refresh tokens — a copy of one is not a second credential, it is the same credential with two owners, and the first profile to refresh it revokes it for every other copy. `--clone-all` (and the dashboard's credential mirroring) therefore drops those OAuth rows from the clone.
L136: The new profile keeps reading the login from the root `~/.hermes/auth.json`, and a token refresh performed inside any profile is written back to root, so all profiles stay signed in. Static API keys are copied as usual. To give a profile its own separate OAuth login, run `hermes -p <name> auth add <provider>` inside it.
L137: ### Clone from a specific profilecite48†​ L138: 
L139:     `
L140: 
L141:     hermes profile create work --clone-from coder
L142: 
L143:     `
L144: 
L145: `--clone-from <source>` selects the source profile directly and implies a config/skills/SOUL clone. Combine it with `--clone-all` when you want a full copy of that source profile:
L146: 
L147:     `
L148: 
L149:     hermes profile create work-backup --clone-from coder --clone-all
L150: 
L151:     `
L152: ### Messaging channels are never cloned (`--clone-channels` to opt in)cite49†​ L153: Every clone — `--clone`, `--clone-from`, `--clone-all`, and the dashboard / Desktop / TUI "clone from profile" option — copies the source without its messaging channels: bot tokens and allowlists (`TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN`, `DISCORD_ALLOWED_USERS`, `WHATSAPP_ENABLED`, `API_SERVER_KEY`, `WEBHOOK_SECRET`, …), the `platforms:` / `telegram:` / `discord:` sections of `config.yaml`, `gateway.multiplex_profiles` / `profile_routes`, and (for `--clone-all`) the pairing store, WhatsApp session and other per-bot state.
L154: Provider and tool API keys, the model block, memory settings, skills and `SOUL.md` are copied as before. The command prints which platforms were left behind.
L155: The reason is that a bot can only belong to one profile: two standalone gateways holding the same token fight over its long-poll, and a cite21†multiplexed gateway parks the duplicate adapter (and `hermes gateway migrate --multiplex` refuses with one duplicate-credential blocker per platform). Configure the new profile's own bots with `hermes -p <name> setup` or the dashboard Messaging page.
L156: 
L157:     `
L158: 
L159:     hermes profile create twin --clone --clone-channels   # keep the source's bots anyway
L160: 
L161:     `
L162: `--clone-channels` is refused when a running multiplexed gateway already serves the source (the copy would be parked immediately) — from the CLI, the dashboard and the TUI alike — and otherwise prints a warning naming the platforms now shared with the source. It is an error without a clone flag. `hermes profile list` prints the same warning for any existing profile whose bot credential is byte-identical to the default's, so older clones surface before they bite.
L163: What counts as a channel setting — the inventory is ownership-based and is judged in the source profile's plugin scope (its private `plugins/` adapters included):
L164:   * every key an adapter declares (tokens, app/client ids, allowlists, allow-all switches, home channels) and every key under its `<PLATFORM>_` prefix, including historical aliases (`WECOM_*`, `SMS_*`/`TWILIO_*`, `QQ_*`, `HASS_*`, `EMAIL_*`);
L165:   * gateway-wide channel policy `GATEWAY_ALLOW_ALL_USERS` / `GATEWAY_ALLOWED_USERS` and the relay enrollment identity `GATEWAY_RELAY_ID` / `GATEWAY_RELAY_SECRET` / `GATEWAY_RELAY_DELIVERY_KEY`;
L166:   * for `--clone-all`, per-bot state files and directories (`platforms/`, pairing ledgers, `google_chat_user_tokens/`, `<platform>_*`).
L167: Credentials that a messaging adapter shares with a non-channel capability — `HASS_TOKEN`/`HASS_URL` (also the Home Assistant tool), `TWILIO_*` (also the telephony skill), `EMAIL_*` (also mail-sending scripts) — are stripped only when the source's gateway would run that adapter (the platform is enabled in its `config.yaml`, or its credential set is complete and not explicitly disabled). A source with `platforms.homeassistant.enabled: false` uses `HASS_TOKEN` as a tool key, so the clone keeps it.
L168: Allowlists and ports under those prefixes are always channel-only and always stripped.
L169: Clones are built in a hidden staging directory beside `profiles/` and published with one rename after the strip, so a running multiplexer (which rescans `profiles/` on create) can never start adapters on a half-copied tree. A symlinked source `.env`/`config.yaml` is materialized as a private copy first — the clone never writes through to the source.
L170: 
L171: Honcho memory + profiles
L172: When Honcho is enabled, clone operations automatically create a dedicated AI peer for the new profile while sharing the same user workspace. Each profile builds its own observations and identity. See cite50†Honcho -- Multi-agent / Profiles for details.
L173: ## Using profilescite51†​ L174: ### Command aliasescite52†​ L175: 
L176: Every profile automatically gets a command alias at `~/.local/bin/<name>`:
L177: 
L178:     `
L179: 
L180:     coder chat                    # chat with the coder agent
L181: 
L182:     coder setup                   # configure coder's settings
L183: 
L184:     coder gateway start           # start coder's gateway
L185: 
L186:     coder doctor                  # check coder's health
L187: 
L188:     coder skills list             # list coder's skills
L189: 
L190:     coder config set model.default anthropic/claude-sonnet-4
L191: 
L192:     `
L193: The alias works with every hermes subcommand — it's just `hermes -p <name>` under the hood.
L194: ### The `-p` flagcite53†​ L195: 
L196: You can also target a profile explicitly with any command:
L197: 
L198:     `
L199: 
L200:     hermes -p coder chat
L201: 
L202:     hermes --profile=coder doctor
L203: 
L204:     hermes chat -p coder -q "hello"    # works in any position
L205: 
L206:     `
L207: ### Sticky default (`hermes profile use`)cite54†​ L208: 
L209:     `
L210: 
L211:     hermes profile use coder
L212: 
L213:     hermes chat                   # now targets coder
L214: 
L215:     hermes tools                  # configures coder's tools
L216: 
L217:     hermes profile use default    # switch back
L218: 
L219:     `
L220: 
L221: Sets a default so plain `hermes` commands target that profile. Like `kubectl config use-context`.
L222: If the sticky profile's directory is deleted by hand, Hermes refuses to run ordinary commands in the default profile instead, since they would read or write the wrong profile's state. Only the ways out still run, with a warning: `hermes profile list`, `hermes profile use default`, and `hermes uninstall` without `--data` or `--full` (those two stay refused; the interactive uninstall menu still offers a full wipe of the default profile behind its confirmation prompts).
L223: ### Knowing where you arecite55†​ L224: 
L225: The CLI always shows which profile is active:
L226: 
L227:   * Prompt: `coder ❯` instead of `❯`
L228:   * Banner: Shows `Profile: coder` on startup
L229:   * `hermes profile`: Shows current profile name, path, model, gateway status
L230: ## Profiles vs workspaces vs sandboxingcite56†​ L231: 
L232: Profiles are often confused with workspaces or sandboxes, but they are different things:
L233: 
L234:   * A profile gives Hermes its own state directory: `config.yaml`, `.env`, `SOUL.md`, sessions, memory, logs, cron jobs, and gateway state.
L235:   * A workspace or working directory is where terminal commands start. That is controlled separately by `terminal.cwd`.
L236:   * A sandbox is what limits filesystem access. Profiles do not sandbox the agent.
L237: On the default `local` terminal backend, the agent still has the same filesystem access as your user account. A profile does not stop it from accessing folders outside the profile directory.
L238: 
L239: If you want a profile to start in a specific project folder, set an explicit absolute `terminal.cwd` in that profile's `config.yaml`:
L240: 
L241:     `
L242: 
L243:     terminal:
L244: 
L245:       backend: local
L246: 
L247:       cwd: /absolute/path/to/project
L248: 
L249:     `
L250: Using `cwd: "."` on the local backend means "the directory Hermes was launched from", not "the profile directory".
L251: 
L252: Also note:
L253: 
L254:   * `SOUL.md` can guide the model, but it does not enforce a workspace boundary.
L255:   * Changes to `SOUL.md` take effect cleanly on a new session. Existing sessions may still be using the old prompt state.
L256:   * Asking the model "what directory are you in?" is not a reliable isolation test. If you need a predictable starting directory for tools, set `terminal.cwd` explicitly.
L257: ## Running gatewayscite57†​ L258: 
L259: Each profile runs its own gateway as a separate process with its own bot token:
L260: 
L261:     `
L262: 
L263:     coder gateway start           # starts coder's gateway
L264: 
L265:     assistant gateway start       # starts assistant's gateway (separate process)
L266: 
L267:     `
L268: ### Different bot tokenscite36†​ L269: 
L270: Each profile has its own `.env` file. Configure a different Telegram/Discord/Slack bot token in each:
L271: 
L272:     `
L273: 
L274:     # Edit coder's tokens
L275: 
L276:     nano ~/.hermes/profiles/coder/.env
L277: 
L278:     # Edit assistant's tokens
L279: 
L280:     nano ~/.hermes/profiles/assistant/.env
L281: 
L282:     `
L283: ### Safety: token lockscite58†​ L284: 
L285: If two profiles accidentally use the same bot token, the second gateway will be blocked with a clear error naming the conflicting profile. Supported for Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, and Signal.
L286: ### Persistent servicescite59†​ L287: 
L288:     `
L289: 
L290:     coder gateway install         # creates hermes-gateway-coder systemd/launchd service
L291: 
L292:     assistant gateway install     # creates hermes-gateway-assistant service
L293: 
L294:     `
L295: 
L296: Each profile gets its own service name. They run independently.
L297: 
L298: Inside the official Docker image
L299: Per-profile gateways are supervised by cite60†s6-overlay†github.com (PID 1 in the container), so `hermes profile create <name>` automatically registers an s6 service slot at `/run/service/gateway-<name>/`. `hermes -p <name> gateway start/stop/restart` dispatches to `s6-svc` instead of spawning a bare process — crashes are auto-restarted and `docker restart` preserves the previously-running set of gateways. See cite61†Per-profile gateway supervision for details.
L300: ## Configuring profilescite62†​ L301: 
L302: Each profile has its own:
L303: 
L304:   * `config.yaml` — model, provider, toolsets, all settings
L305:   * `.env` — API keys, bot tokens
L306:   * `SOUL.md` — personality and instructions
L307: 
L308:     `
L309: 
L310:     coder config set model.default anthropic/claude-sonnet-4
L311: 
L312:     echo "You are a focused coding assistant." > ~/.hermes/profiles/coder/SOUL.md
L313: 
L314:     `
L315: If you want this profile to work in a specific project by default, also set its own `terminal.cwd`:
L316: 
L317:     `
L318: 
L319:     coder config set terminal.cwd /absolute/path/to/project
L320: 
L321:     `
L322: ### From the dashboardcite63†​ L323: 
L324: The cite64†web dashboard is a machine-level surface that can manage any profile's config, API keys, skills, MCPs, and model via the profile switcher in its sidebar — no per-profile dashboard needed. `coder dashboard` routes to the machine dashboard with the `coder` profile preselected. The dashboard's Chat tab also follows the switcher, spawning a conversation under the selected profile's home.
L325: Note: "Set as active" on the dashboard's Profiles page is the sticky default for future CLI/gateway runs (same as `hermes profile use`) — to edit a profile from the dashboard, use the switcher instead.
L326: ## Updatingcite65†​ L327: 
L328: `hermes update` pulls code once (shared) and syncs new bundled skills to all profiles automatically:
L329: 
L330:     `
L331: 
L332:     hermes update
L333: 
L334:     # → Code updated (12 commits)
L335: 
L336:     # → Skills synced: default (up to date), coder (+2 new), assistant (+2 new)
L337: 
L338:     `
L339: 
L340: User-modified skills are never overwritten.
L341: Dependency preparation reads every profile's `config.yaml` to compute the plugin set the shared environment must carry. A profile whose `config.yaml` does not parse (or whose `plugins` / `memory` sections have the wrong shape) fails that step for the whole install — see cite66†Dependency preparation and preservation .
L342: ## Managing profilescite67†​ L343: 
L344:     `
L345: 
L346:     hermes profile list           # show all profiles with status
L347: 
L348:     hermes profile show coder     # detailed info for one profile
L349: 
L350:     hermes profile rename coder dev-bot   # rename (updates alias; removes the old name's gateway service)
L351: 
L352:     hermes profile migrate-identity coder dev-bot   # retry a rename's identity migration
L353: 
L354:     hermes profile purge-identity dev-bot   # retry a delete's identity purge
L355:     hermes profile export coder   # pack into coder.tar.gz (shareable; keys stripped)
L356: 
L357:     hermes profile import coder.tar.gz   # install an archive as a new profile
L358: 
L359:     `
L360: In chat, the same two live as `/export` and `/import` — and in the desktop app as ⌘K → Export/Import profile…. See cite68†Sharing a profile .
L361: ### Naming the default profilecite69†​ L362: 
L363: The default profile's internal ID is always `default` — it can't be truly renamed because `~/.hermes` is the installation root. Renaming it instead sets a display name, which UI surfaces show in place of the bare ID:
L364: 
L365:     `
L366: 
L367:     hermes profile rename default Harumesu   # Unicode fine: 小助手
L368: 
L369:     `
L370: The display name appears in `hermes profile list`/`show`, the `/profile` chat command, the dashboard, and the desktop app (including the Bot Mode roster). It is presentation-only: `-p default`, service names, cron jobs, and every other reference keep using the canonical `default` ID. It is stored as `display_name` in `~/.hermes/profile.yaml`; remove that line to revert. Named profiles can carry a `display_name` too (it survives a real rename), but `rename` for them still renames the profile itself.
L371: ## Deleting a profilecite70†​ L372: 
L373:     `
L374: 
L375:     hermes profile delete coder
L376: 
L377:     `
L378: 
L379: This stops the gateway, removes the systemd/launchd service, removes the command alias, and deletes all profile data. You'll be asked to type the profile name to confirm.
L380: 
L381: Use `--yes` to skip confirmation: `hermes profile delete coder --yes`
L382: 
L383: note
L384: 
L385: You cannot delete the default profile (`~/.hermes`). To remove everything, use `hermes uninstall`.
L386: ## Tab completioncite71†​ L387: 
L388:     `
L389: 
L390:     # Bash
L391: 
L392:     eval "$(hermes completion bash)"
L393: 
L394:     # Zsh
L395: 
L396:     eval "$(hermes completion zsh)"
L397: 
L398:     `
L399: 
L400: Add the line to your `~/.bashrc` or `~/.zshrc` for persistent completion. Completes profile names after `-p`, profile subcommands, and top-level commands.
L401: ## How it workscite72†​ L402: 
L403: Profiles use the `HERMES_HOME` environment variable. When you run `coder chat`, the wrapper script sets `HERMES_HOME=~/.hermes/profiles/coder` before launching hermes. Since 119+ files in the codebase resolve paths via `get_hermes_home()`, Hermes state automatically scopes to the profile's directory — config, sessions, memory, skills, state database, gateway PID, logs, and cron jobs.
L404: This is separate from terminal working directory. Tool execution starts from `terminal.cwd` (or the launch directory when `cwd: "."` on the local backend), not automatically from `HERMES_HOME`.
L405: On host installs, tool subprocesses keep your real OS-user `HOME` by default so existing CLI credentials under `~` keep working across profiles. Profile data is isolated by `HERMES_HOME`, not by changing `HOME`. Container backends still use `{HERMES_HOME}/home` for persistent tool state, and host users who need strict per-profile tool config can opt in with `terminal.home_mode: profile`.
L406: 
L407: This means two things that are easy to mix up:
L408:   * `HERMES_HOME` is the profile boundary. It controls Hermes config, `.env`, memory, sessions, skills, logs, cron jobs, gateway state, and other Hermes data.
L409:   * `HOME` is the operating-system/user home that external CLIs expect. On host installs, Hermes keeps it as the real user home by default so tools like `git`, `ssh`, `gh`, `az`, `npm`, Claude Code, and Codex find the same credentials they use in your normal shell.
L410: The tradeoff is that host profiles share normal user-level CLI state by default. If you need separate CLI identities per profile, set `terminal.home_mode: profile` in that profile's `config.yaml`. In that mode Hermes launches tool subprocesses with `HOME={HERMES_HOME}/home`; you then need to initialize or link the profile-specific `~/.ssh`, `~/.gitconfig`, `~/.config/gh`, cloud CLI auth, Claude/Codex auth, npm state, and similar files inside that profile home.
L411: Hermes also exposes `HERMES_REAL_HOME` to subprocesses so scripts can still find the actual account home when `home_mode: profile` is active.
L412: 
L413: The default profile is simply `~/.hermes` itself. No migration needed — existing installs work identically.
L414: ## Sharing a profilecite68†​ L415: 
L416: A profile you built on one machine can go to another — your own workstation, a teammate's laptop, or the community. Two paths:
L417: 
L418: Send a file. `/export` packs the profile into one `.tar.gz` — skills, memory, persona, crons, plugins, settings, and (from the desktop) your theme and layout. API keys are stripped. The recipient runs `/import`.
L419: Machine-specific PM state is not portable. Export, import, and distribution install exclude `installs/`, `tools/`, and `cache/` at a profile's root. Backup and restore apply the same rule to the default home and named profiles. Older archives cannot replace the destination machine's PM selections or tools. Files such as `plugins/example/facts.json` and `skills/example/tools/helper.py` remain user data and are preserved.
L420: Install dependencies on the destination through cite73†PM , rather than copying environments.
L421: 
L422:     `
L423: 
L424:     # In chat, run /export, hand over the file, and they run /import on it
L425: 
L426:     hermes profile export coder
L427: 
L428:     hermes profile import ./coder.tar.gz --name coder
L429: 
L430:     `
L431: Publish a distribution. Package the profile as a git repository so recipients install it with one command and pull versioned updates later. Carries the SOUL, config, skills, cron jobs, and MCP connections; credentials, memories, and sessions stay per-machine.
L432: 
L433:     `
L434: 
L435:     # Install a whole agent from a git repo
L436: 
L437:     hermes profile install github.com/you/research-bot --alias
L438: 
L439:     # Update later when the author ships a new version (keeps your memories + .env)
L440:     hermes profile update research-bot
L441: 
L442:     `
L443: Use an export file for a one-time handoff or a move; use a distribution for an agent you'll keep shipping. See cite20†Profile Distributions: Share a Whole Agent for both — the comparison table, authoring, publishing, update semantics, and the security model.
L444:

**Yes: shared service, separate conversation state, owner-scoped tools, and isolated execution when work needs it.** A permanently running Hermes instance per person is unnecessary for that design.

| Layer | Scope |
|---|---|
| Workspace tenant | Installation, team configuration, membership, billing |
| Conversation | Private DM owner, or authorized channel/thread audience |
| Stored state | Conversation history plus separately scoped memory, files, credentials, browser sessions |
| Execution | An active run bound to one tenant and authorized account owner |
| Compute | Shared trusted coordinator; isolated workers started/reused for active private runs |

This **changes the previous compute-isolation contract**: personal data is no longer exclusively processed inside each user’s isolated full Hermes runtime. Confidentiality instead depends on access checks throughout the shared service and its tools. This is a viable architecture choice if those controls are comprehensive.

Five pitfalls matter:

1. **A channel is an audience, not the whole workspace.** Private channels and Slack Connect make “all team context” unsafe. Threads inherit their channel’s audience.
2. **History separation alone is insufficient.** Memory, session recall, learned skills, file tools, search indexes, caches, logs, queues, and artifacts must also respect scope.
3. **Private execution needs private observations.** A channel agent cannot call Sahan’s account and ingest the raw result into its shared conversation. Use a separate private run/session and release an approved output.
4. **Worker ownership must come from trusted routing.** Bind tenant, owner, allowed resources, action approval, and publication audience outside model-generated arguments. Reset reused workers and restore only the current owner’s state.
5. **The shared coordinator cannot have unrestricted agent tools.** Host terminal/filesystem access or unscoped recall can bypass application checks. Disable those surfaces or execute them behind the scoped broker.

Keep durable personal state even when private workers stop. Shared Hermes code and model access do not imply shared conversation memory, credentials, or browser sessions.

**Yes. We can build yyot as one logical assistant per workspace, with private DM sessions and shared channel sessions. A permanent Hermes instance per user isn’t inherently required.**

Each user’s DM gives them a private conversation. The backend must preserve that privacy when retrieving memory, accessing accounts, and executing tools.

For v1, I’d treat **each Slack workspace as a tenant**:

| Conversation | Context available to that conversation |
|---|---|
| Workspace A → Sahan’s DM | Sahan’s private history and authorized resources |
| Workspace A → Nishank’s DM | Nishank’s private history and authorized resources |
| Workspace A → `#project` | That channel’s shared discussions, documents, and approved results |
| Workspace A → private `#finance` | Context restricted to that channel’s audience |
| Workspace B → any conversation | Workspace B’s authorized context, isolated from A |

**The architecture would have five responsibilities:**

1. **Route by verified identity.** Every request carries its workspace, sender, and conversation. These come from authenticated Slack events.
2. **Load the appropriate conversation.** DMs load personal context; channels and threads load shared context. A channel conversation cannot retrieve somebody’s DM history.
3. **Keep persistent data scoped.** Memory, files, browser sessions, and credentials retain their owner or audience. Switching conversations must also switch which resources are accessible.
4. **Run tools with limited access.** Shared infrastructure coordinates requests. Browser and generated-code work runs in isolated environments with access only to the authorized owner’s resources. These workers can start when needed.
5. **Deliver to the correct audience.** Private account observations stay in a private execution session. Only owner-approved content enters the channel’s shared conversation.

For example, Sahan could ask in `#project` to prepare a report using his private account. yyot handles the account work privately, sends him the result in a DM, and publishes the content he approves. Nishank can contribute requirements without acquiring Sahan’s account access.

**When Prateek joins:** joining Workspace A gives him access according to its channel membership, without exposing other users’ DMs or accounts. Installing yyot in his own Workspace B creates another tenant with separate context and resources.

Hermes already supports separate DM sessions and shared channel/thread sessions. However, its profile routing does **not** implement end-user authorization, and profiles do not sandbox filesystem access. Those protections still require yyot integration. [Session behavior](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/sessions/#shared-vs-isolated-group-sessions), [authorization boundary](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/developer-guide/multiplexing-gateway/#non-goals), [sandboxing distinction](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/profiles/#profiles-vs-workspaces-vs-sandboxing).

**Yes. We can build yyot as one logical assistant per workspace, with private DM sessions and shared channel sessions. A permanent Hermes instance per user isn’t inherently required.**

Each user’s DM gives them a private conversation. The backend must preserve that privacy when retrieving memory, accessing accounts, and executing tools.

For v1, I’d treat **each Slack workspace as a tenant**:

| Conversation | Context available to that conversation |
|---|---|
| Workspace A → Sahan’s DM | Sahan’s private history and authorized resources |
| Workspace A → Nishank’s DM | Nishank’s private history and authorized resources |
| Workspace A → `#project` | That channel’s shared discussions, documents, and approved results |
| Workspace A → private `#finance` | Context restricted to that channel’s audience |
| Workspace B → any conversation | Workspace B’s authorized context, isolated from A |

**The architecture would have five responsibilities:**

1. **Route by verified identity.** Every request carries its workspace, sender, and conversation. These come from authenticated Slack events.
2. **Load the appropriate conversation.** DMs load personal context; channels and threads load shared context. A channel conversation cannot retrieve somebody’s DM history.
3. **Keep persistent data scoped.** Memory, files, browser sessions, and credentials retain their owner or audience. Switching conversations must also switch which resources are accessible.
4. **Run tools with limited access.** Shared infrastructure coordinates requests. Browser and generated-code work runs in isolated environments with access only to the authorized owner’s resources. These workers can start when needed.
5. **Deliver to the correct audience.** Private account observations stay in a private execution session. Only owner-approved content enters the channel’s shared conversation.

For example, Sahan could ask in `#project` to prepare a report using his private account. yyot handles the account work privately, sends him the result in a DM, and publishes the content he approves. Nishank can contribute requirements without acquiring Sahan’s account access.

**When Prateek joins:** joining Workspace A gives him access according to its channel membership, without exposing other users’ DMs or accounts. Installing yyot in his own Workspace B creates another tenant with separate context and resources.

why couldn't one agent in multi-tenant could work?

**It can. A separate Hermes instance per tenant was an isolation option I suggested, not a technical requirement.**

We could run **one shared Hermes-based service serving many tenants**, with separate sessions and permissions:

| Shared | Kept separate |
|---|---|
| Agent software and orchestration | Each tenant’s data and configuration |
| Model service | Each conversation’s history and memory |
| Hosting infrastructure | Users’ credentials, browser sessions, and private files |

For every request, yyot would identify the tenant, user, and conversation, then load **only the context and tools that request is authorized to access**. Generated code would execute in an isolated worker without access to the shared service’s databases or other users’ resources.

The distinction is **one shared agent engine versus one shared conversation and unrestricted access to everyone’s data**.

The tradeoff: fewer deployments, but more responsibility in yyot’s authorization, memory retrieval, and execution controls. Hermes’s routing alone doesn’t implement those permissions. [Hermes authorization boundary](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/developer-guide/multiplexing-gateway/#non-goals)

**One shared service is a viable architecture. We haven’t established a reason that yyot requires an instance per tenant.**

name: "pdf"
description: "Read, create, inspect, render, and verify PDF files where visual layout matters, including fillable AcroForms. Use Poppler rendering plus Python tools such as reportlab, pdfplumber, and pypdf for generation and extraction."
---

# PDF Skill

## When To Use

- Read or review PDF content where layout and visuals matter.
- Create PDFs programmatically with reliable formatting.
- Fill and validate interactive PDF forms.
- Validate final rendering before delivery.

## Tools + Contract Requirements

Immediately before the first create/edit authoring command, run `mark_artifact_operation_started.mjs` successfully exactly once using the command below. Do not run it for read-only work. For edits, replace `create` with `edit`; adjust the expected count and output format to match the requested outputs.

```bash
node container_tools/mark_artifact_operation_started.mjs --operation-kind create --expected-output-count 1 --output-format pdf
```

## Workflow

1. Prefer visual review: render PDF pages to PNGs and inspect them.
   - Use `pdftoppm` from the bundled runtime or system Poppler when available.
   - If unavailable, install Poppler or ask the user to review the output locally.
2. Use `reportlab` to generate PDFs when creating new documents.
3. Use `pdfplumber` or `pypdf` for text extraction and quick checks; do not rely on text extraction for layout fidelity.
4. After each meaningful update, re-render pages and verify alignment, spacing, and legibility.

## Fill And Validate AcroForms

Visual review alone is not a correctness check for a fillable PDF. A page `/Widget` annotation can render a value from its appearance stream while the canonical `/AcroForm/Fields` tree is missing or contains a stale value.

1. Keep the result interactive by default; set `flatten=True` only when the user explicitly requests a completed, static form. Preserve the source PDF, and do not flatten a signed PDF without an explicit workflow decision.
2. Inspect both representations before filling: enumerate fields from `reader.get_fields()` and `/Widget` annotations from every page's `/Annots`, following `/Parent` and `/Kids`. If a widget and a canonical field have the same name but are distinct objects with no `/Parent` relationship, do not call `reattach_fields()` blindly: it can create a second top-level field with the same name. Report the ambiguity or produce a static result.
3. Recover genuinely orphaned widgets, fill all pages, and write the result with `pypdf`:

```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter
from pypdf.generic import NameObject

reader = PdfReader(input_pdf)
writer = PdfWriter()
writer.clone_document_from_reader(reader)

# Restores widgets that are missing from /AcroForm/Fields.
writer.reattach_fields()
fields = writer.get_fields() or {}
missing = set(expected_values) - set(fields)
if missing:
    raise ValueError(f"Form fields not found after repair: {sorted(missing)}")

values_to_write = dict(expected_values)
if flatten:
    # Paint every existing value before removing every widget.
    values_to_write = {
        name: field.get("/V", "/Off" if field.get("/FT") == "/Btn" else "")
        for name, field in fields.items()
    }
    values_to_write.update(expected_values)

writer.update_page_form_field_values(
    None, values_to_write, auto_regenerate=False, flatten=flatten
)

if flatten:
    # pypdf's flatten=True paints appearances but does not remove widgets.
    writer.remove_annotations(subtypes="/Widget")
    writer.root_object.pop(NameObject("/AcroForm"), None)

with open(output_pdf, "wb") as stream:
    writer.write(stream)
```

4. Reopen the written PDF before delivery. For an interactive result, require every expected field to be present in `get_fields()` with the expected `/V`, enumerate page widgets again, and confirm their effective `/V` (the widget value or inherited `/Parent` value) agrees. Confirm each updated widget has a non-empty `/AP` `/N` appearance and render the final pages to catch stale or clipped appearances. Do not rely on `/NeedAppearances` or a successful PNG render as proof that logical field data was updated.
5. For a flattened result, require zero `/Widget` annotations and no remaining `/AcroForm` field tree after reopening, then render the final pages. Keep an editable copy when the user may need to revise the form.

## Temp And Output Conventions

- Use `tmp/pdfs/` for intermediate files; delete them when done.
- Write final artifacts under `output/pdf/` when working in this repo.
- Keep filenames stable and descriptive.

## Dependencies

Prefer the Codex bundled workspace/runtime dependencies when available. The primary runtime is expected to include:

- Python packages: `reportlab`, `pdfplumber`, `pypdf`
- Rendering tools: `pdftoppm` and `pdfinfo` from Poppler

If a dependency is missing, install only what is needed.

Python packages:

```bash
uv pip install reportlab pdfplumber pypdf
```

If `uv` is unavailable:

```bash
python3 -m pip install reportlab pdfplumber pypdf
```

System tools for rendering:

```bash
# macOS (Homebrew)
brew install poppler

# Ubuntu/Debian
sudo apt-get install -y poppler-utils
```

If installation is not possible in this environment, tell the user which dependency is missing and how to install it locally.

## Environment

No required environment variables.

## Rendering Command

```bash
pdftoppm -png "$INPUT_PDF" "$OUTPUT_PREFIX"
```

## Quality Expectations

- Maintain polished visual design: consistent typography, spacing, margins, and section hierarchy.
- Avoid rendering issues: clipped text, overlapping elements, broken tables, black squares, or unreadable glyphs.
- Charts, tables, and images must be sharp, aligned, and clearly labeled.
- Use ASCII hyphens only. Avoid U+2011 and other Unicode dashes.
- Citations and references must be human-readable; never leave tool tokens or placeholder strings.

## Final Checks

- Do not deliver until the latest PNG inspection shows zero visual or formatting defects.
- Confirm headers, footers, page numbering, and section transitions look polished.
- Keep intermediate files organized or remove them after final approval.

## Final response citations

Place `:codex-file-citation{...}` inline in prose, not in a trailing list. Use `purpose="source"` for Q&A/no-op and `purpose="output"` for create/edit.

- [HARD REQUIREMENT] Create/edit: cite each final PDF exactly once with a plain output citation. Summarize representative changes; do not cite every page or add a separate filename, path, or Markdown link. Example: `Created :codex-file-citation{path="/abs/path/report.pdf" purpose="output"}, with the completed analysis and appendix.`
- Q&A/no-op: do not edit or re-export. Inspect the complete relevant pages, preserve material headings, table/figure labels, footnotes, sources, and sample sizes, and cite each source PDF once with a plain source citation.

PDF citations currently support only plain file citations. Do not add `artifact_kind`, `page_number`, or other locators. Never cite rendered PNGs, scratch files, builders, or QA intermediates unless asked.

# PDF Skill

## When To Use

- Read or review PDF content where layout and visuals matter.
- Create PDFs programmatically with reliable formatting.
- Fill and validate interactive PDF forms.
- Validate final rendering before delivery.

## Tools + Contract Requirements

Immediately before the first create/edit authoring command, run `mark_artifact_operation_started.mjs` successfully exactly once using the command below. Do not run it for read-only work. For edits, replace `create` with `edit`; adjust the expected count and output format to match the requested outputs.

```bash
node container_tools/mark_artifact_operation_started.mjs --operation-kind create --expected-output-count 1 --output-format pdf
```

## Workflow

1. Prefer visual review: render PDF pages to PNGs and inspect them.
   - Use `pdftoppm` from the bundled runtime or system Poppler when available.
   - If unavailable, install Poppler or ask the user to review the output locally.
2. Use `reportlab` to generate PDFs when creating new documents.
3. Use `pdfplumber` or `pypdf` for text extraction and quick checks; do not rely on text extraction for layout fidelity.
4. After each meaningful update, re-render pages and verify alignment, spacing, and legibility.

## Fill And Validate AcroForms

Visual review alone is not a correctness check for a fillable PDF. A page `/Widget` annotation can render a value from its appearance stream while the canonical `/AcroForm/Fields` tree is missing or contains a stale value.

1. Keep the result interactive by default; set `flatten=True` only when the user explicitly requests a completed, static form. Preserve the source PDF, and do not flatten a signed PDF without an explicit workflow decision.
2. Inspect both representations before filling: enumerate fields from `reader.get_fields()` and `/Widget` annotations from every page's `/Annots`, following `/Parent` and `/Kids`. If a widget and a canonical field have the same name but are distinct objects with no `/Parent` relationship, do not call `reattach_fields()` blindly: it can create a second top-level field with the same name. Report the ambiguity or produce a static result.
3. Recover genuinely orphaned widgets, fill all pages, and write the result with `pypdf`:

```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter
from pypdf.generic import NameObject

reader = PdfReader(input_pdf)
writer = PdfWriter()
writer.clone_document_from_reader(reader)

# Restores widgets that are missing from /AcroForm/Fields.
writer.reattach_fields()
fields = writer.get_fields() or {}
missing = set(expected_values) - set(fields)
if missing:
    raise ValueError(f"Form fields not found after repair: {sorted(missing)}")

values_to_write = dict(expected_values)
if flatten:
    # Paint every existing value before removing every widget.
    values_to_write = {
        name: field.get("/V", "/Off" if field.get("/FT") == "/Btn" else "")
        for name, field in fields.items()
    }
    values_to_write.update(expected_values)

writer.update_page_form_field_values(
    None, values_to_write, auto_regenerate=False, flatten=flatten
)

if flatten:
    # pypdf's flatten=True paints appearances but does not remove widgets.
    writer.remove_annotations(subtypes="/Widget")
    writer.root_object.pop(NameObject("/AcroForm"), None)

with open(output_pdf, "wb") as stream:
    writer.write(stream)
```

4. Reopen the written PDF before delivery. For an interactive result, require every expected field to be present in `get_fields()` with the expected `/V`, enumerate page widgets again, and confirm their effective `/V` (the widget value or inherited `/Parent` value) agrees. Confirm each updated widget has a non-empty `/AP` `/N` appearance and render the final pages to catch stale or clipped appearances. Do not rely on `/NeedAppearances` or a successful PNG render as proof that logical field data was updated.

description: "Read, create, inspect, render, and verify PDF files where visual layout matters, including fillable AcroForms. Use Poppler rendering plus Python tools such as reportlab, pdfplumber, and pypdf for generation and extraction."
---

# PDF Skill

## When To Use

- Read or review PDF content where layout and visuals matter.
- Create PDFs programmatically with reliable formatting.
- Fill and validate interactive PDF forms.
- Validate final rendering before delivery.

## Tools + Contract Requirements

Immediately before the first create/edit authoring command, run `mark_artifact_operation_started.mjs` successfully exactly once using the command below. Do not run it for read-only work. For edits, replace `create` with `edit`; adjust the expected count and output format to match the requested outputs.

```bash
node container_tools/mark_artifact_operation_started.mjs --operation-kind create --expected-output-count 1 --output-format pdf
```

## Workflow

1. Prefer visual review: render PDF pages to PNGs and inspect them.
   - Use `pdftoppm` from the bundled runtime or system Poppler when available.
   - If unavailable, install Poppler or ask the user to review the output locally.
2. Use `reportlab` to generate PDFs when creating new documents.
3. Use `pdfplumber` or `pypdf` for text extraction and quick checks; do not rely on text extraction for layout fidelity.
4. After each meaningful update, re-render pages and verify alignment, spacing, and legibility.

## Fill And Validate AcroForms

Visual review alone is not a correctness check for a fillable PDF. A page `/Widget` annotation can render a value from its appearance stream while the canonical `/AcroForm/Fields` tree is missing or contains a stale value.

1. Keep the result interactive by default; set `flatten=True` only when the user explicitly requests a completed, static form. Preserve the source PDF, and do not flatten a signed PDF without an explicit workflow decision.
2. Inspect both representations before filling: enumerate fields from `reader.get_fields()` and `/Widget` annotations from every page's `/Annots`, following `/Parent` and `/Kids`. If a widget and a canonical field have the same name but are distinct objects with no `/Parent` relationship, do not call `reattach_fields()` blindly: it can create a second top-level field with the same name. Report the ambiguity or produce a static result.
3. Recover genuinely orphaned widgets, fill all pages, and write the result with `pypdf`:

```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter
from pypdf.generic import NameObject

reader = PdfReader(input_pdf)
writer = PdfWriter()
writer.clone_document_from_reader(reader)

# Restores widgets that are missing from /AcroForm/Fields.
writer.reattach_fields()
fields = writer.get_fields() or {}
missing = set(expected_values) - set(fields)
if missing:
    raise ValueError(f"Form fields not found after repair: {sorted(missing)}")

values_to_write = dict(expected_values)
if flatten:
    # Paint every existing value before removing every widget.
    values_to_write = {
        name: field.get("/V", "/Off" if field.get("/FT") == "/Btn" else "")
        for name, field in fields.items()
    }
    values_to_write.update(expected_values)

writer.update_page_form_field_values(
    None, values_to_write, auto_regenerate=False, flatten=flatten
)

if flatten:
    # pypdf's flatten=True paints appearances but does not remove widgets.
    writer.remove_annotations(subtypes="/Widget")
    writer.root_object.pop(NameObject("/AcroForm"), None)

with open(output_pdf, "wb") as stream:
    writer.write(stream)
```

4. Reopen the written PDF before delivery. For an interactive result, require every expected field to be present in `get_fields()` with the expected `/V`, enumerate page widgets again, and confirm their effective `/V` (the widget value or inherited `/Parent` value) agrees. Confirm each updated widget has a non-empty `/AP` `/N` appearance and render the final pages to catch stale or clipped appearances. Do not rely on `/NeedAppearances` or a successful PNG render as proof that logical field data was updated.
5. For a flattened result, require zero `/Widget` annotations and no remaining `/AcroForm` field tree after reopening, then render the final pages. Keep an editable copy when the user may need to revise the form.

## Temp And Output Conventions

- Use `tmp/pdfs/` for intermediate files; delete them when done.
- Write final artifacts under `output/pdf/` when working in this repo.
- Keep filenames stable and descriptive.

## Dependencies

Prefer the Codex bundled workspace/runtime dependencies when available. The primary runtime is expected to include:

- Python packages: `reportlab`, `pdfplumber`, `pypdf`
- Rendering tools: `pdftoppm` and `pdfinfo` from Poppler

If a dependency is missing, install only what is needed.

Python packages:

```bash
uv pip install reportlab pdfplumber pypdf
```

If `uv` is unavailable:

```bash
python3 -m pip install reportlab pdfplumber pypdf
```

System tools for rendering:

```bash
# macOS (Homebrew)
brew install poppler

# Ubuntu/Debian
sudo apt-get install -y poppler-utils
```

If installation is not possible in this environment, tell the user which dependency is missing and how to install it locally.

## Environment

No required environment variables.

## Rendering Command

```bash
pdftoppm -png "$INPUT_PDF" "$OUTPUT_PREFIX"
```

## Quality Expectations

- Maintain polished visual design: consistent typography, spacing, margins, and section hierarchy.
- Avoid rendering issues: clipped text, overlapping elements, broken tables, black squares, or unreadable glyphs.
- Charts, tables, and images must be sharp, aligned, and clearly labeled.
- Use ASCII hyphens only. Avoid U+2011 and other Unicode dashes.
- Citations and references must be human-readable; never leave tool tokens or placeholder strings.

## Final Checks

- Do not deliver until the latest PNG inspection shows zero visual or formatting defects.
- Confirm headers, footers, page numbering, and section transitions look polished.
- Keep intermediate files organized or remove them after final approval.

## Final response citations

Place `:codex-file-citation{...}` inline in prose, not in a trailing list. Use `purpose="source"` for Q&A/no-op and `purpose="output"` for create/edit.

- [HARD REQUIREMENT] Create/edit: cite each final PDF exactly once with a plain output citation. Summarize representative changes; do not cite every page or add a separate filename, path, or Markdown link. Example: `Created :codex-file-citation{path="/abs/path/report.pdf" purpose="output"}, with the completed analysis and appendix.`
- Q&A/no-op: do not edit or re-export. Inspect the complete relevant pages, preserve material headings, table/figure labels, footnotes, sources, and sample sizes, and cite each source PDF once with a plain source citation.

PDF citations currently support only plain file citations. Do not add `artifact_kind`, `page_number`, or other locators. Never cite rendered PNGs, scratch files, builders, or QA intermediates unless asked.

Pages: 2
PAGE 1
Instinct-style Browser-use + Credentials Management
Build one Instinct-style chatbot app for browser-use and credentials management. The user asks for 
a task on a website, and the assistant gets it done. Keep the build focused on these two capabilities.
Check out zonko.ai and luffy.so to know more about us.
Desired user experience
 The user asks for something in plain language. The assistant understands the request, asks only 
for details that matter, and starts the work.
 When access is needed, offer a clear, secure way to provide it: API key, OAuth/connect link, 
browser login, or card details. Keep secrets out of chat and model inputs. Store access securely so
the user does not have to provide it again for each task.
 Support authenticator-based 2FA: the user provides the TOTP setup key once through a secure 
input, and the assistant generates codes when login requires them. Other verification methods 
may still need user action. Let the user remove stored access.
 The browser runs in the background. The user should not need to watch it or manage clicks. Give 
brief updates when useful; ask for help only when necessary. If access expires or a task fails, 
explain what is needed and resume without losing the request.
 Reuse saved credentials and sessions across tasks and fresh browser runs. Check the actual result
before saying the task is done.
The same assistant should handle requests across different websites, not just a preselected website 
or scripted flow. Use browser-use to work through unfamiliar pages. Be clear about unsupported 
cases. For signing into the chatbot app itself, keep it simple: Google sign-in only.
Guidance and reference experience
Suggestion: Feel free to use any 3rd party hosted options. User experience is more important. For 
example: use existing platforms like browser-use, Kernel or Browserbase to solve for browser use.
To get more clarity on the assignment, play around with Instinct. If you don’t have it, you can use this 
invite.
Try this prompt with Instinct to get an understanding of the experience:
“Can you login into my gmail and use it for authenticating to vercel? Use my openrouter api key to 
generate a video. Can you repeat my last order on swiggy to the same address?”
What we will evaluate
 Taste and UX. Does it feel smooth and effortless to use? Can the user ask naturally, connect once 
and get a result without thinking about the browser or technical details?
PAGE 2
 Credentials thinking. Did you explore good ways to collect, persist and reuse access, including 
2FA? Is the experience safe and easy to revoke?
 Reliability. Can the user trust the assistant to get tasks done consistently, across repeated 
attempts and different websites? When something blocks it, does it explain plainly and recover 
without making the user start over?
 Judgment. Are the choices thoughtful and the limits honest? Can you explain the tradeoffs and 
what you would improve next?
Send us
A runnable repo, a deployed link, a short demo recording (~2 minutes), and a brief note on your 
access-management choices and known limits. Use any stack. We care more about one smooth, 
working experience than the amount of code.
Note: We understand this assignment requires a lot of time to get it right on the whole. We are 
looking to evaluate your problem solving skills with this assignment. So, give it your best accordingly.
